protection](#chapter-12-winding-homotopy-and-topological-protection)[Chapter
14 --- Fusion and topological charge
→](#chapter-14-fusion-and-topological-charge)

## Chapter 14 --- Fusion and topological charge

::: {.chapter-intro math-section=""}
Consider two particles enclosed within a region whose interior an
outside observer cannot resolve. Each external measurement then reports
one coarse property: the type of source the region presents as a whole.

Local rearrangements of the particles inside leave that external report
unchanged. The region carries a label fixed by all such local
rearrangements.

The previous chapter established that exchanging two such particles can
rotate an internal state. This chapter identifies the structure of that
state.

The discussion begins with a multiplication table describing how
particle labels combine. It then introduces two diagrammatic operations:
an [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-move, which changes the grouping of
particles, and an [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-move, which exchanges two
particles.

**Assumes:** Chapter 13 --- exchange can act as a matrix on a degenerate
space of states. **Introduces:** topological charge, fusion rules and
their coefficients [\\(N\_{ab}\^{c}\\)]{.math .inline}, fusion spaces
and fusion trees, the [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-move (regrouping) and
[\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-move (exchange), quantum dimension, and the
consistency conditions those data must satisfy. **Used later in:**
Fibonacci anyons (Chapter 15), string nets (Chapter 18), and the
architecture chapters; the same [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}- and
[\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-data are re-derived categorically in Appendices
D--E. **Watch:** a fusion coefficient counts *states*, not
probabilities; the amplitudes come later from the [\\(F\\)]{.math
.inline}- and [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-matrices.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Topological charge as a locally invariant label

Consider a loop enclosing several quasiparticles, where a quasiparticle
is an emergent particle-like excitation of a many-body system. An
observer outside the loop can characterize the type of source contained
inside it. Operations performed locally within the loop cannot change
that external characterization.

This characterization is called a charge. More specifically, it is often
called a topological charge because a perturbation confined to one
location cannot change it. Throughout this chapter, charge denotes this
collective label of the enclosed region.

Possible charges carry symbols such as [\\(a\\)]{.math .inline},
[\\(b\\)]{.math .inline}, and [\\(c\\)]{.math .inline}. Every allowed
local operation preserves the total charge of an isolated system: a
region of total charge [\\(a\\)]{.math .inline} keeps that label under
all local operations, and never acquires a different total charge
[\\(b\\)]{.math .inline} through them.

A region containing no residual excitation is assigned the distinguished
label [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline}, called the vacuum charge. The symbol
[\\(1\\)]{.math .inline} is a charge label rather than an ordinary
numerical value.

An operation reaching in from outside can change the total charge by
acting on the region nonlocally. Restricting to local operations
recovers the sector structure of the previous two chapters: each charge
label names one sector, and allowed local operations never connect
states of different total charge.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Fusion of two charge labels

Two regions can be combined and treated as a single larger region. The
total charge of the combined region need not be unique. Charges
[\\(a\\)]{.math .inline} and [\\(b\\)]{.math .inline} can admit several
possible total charges.

The fusion product records these allowed totals:

[\\\[ a\\times b=\\sum_c N\_{ab}\^{c}\\,c. \\\]]{.math .display}

The quantity [\\(N\_{ab}\^{c}\\)]{.math .inline} is a nonnegative
integer called a fusion coefficient. The value zero means that total
charge [\\(c\\)]{.math .inline} is forbidden. The value one means that
there is one independent way for [\\(a\\)]{.math .inline} and
[\\(b\\)]{.math .inline} to have total charge [\\(c\\)]{.math .inline}.
The value two means that there are two independent ways to obtain the
same externally visible total charge [\\(c\\)]{.math .inline}.

This combination process is called fusion. Fusion names the total charge
seen when the two particles are treated as one composite region; the
quasiparticles persist, and no collision debris is implied.

The plus sign in the fusion product lists alternative allowed totals. It
records the set of possible measurement outcomes, not a statistical
mixture already prepared in the system, and not a simultaneous
realization of every listed result. A quantum state becomes a
superposition of these alternatives only when the full experimental
configuration supports coherence between them.

A fusion product therefore lists allowed total charges while leaving the
prepared superposition and its probability distribution to be specified
separately.
:::

:::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Fusion rules of the Ising model

The Ising model contains three charge labels: [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline},
[\\(\\psi\\)]{.math .inline}, and [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline}. Its
fusion products are

[\\\[ 1\\times a=a,\\qquad \\psi\\times\\psi=1,\\qquad
\\psi\\times\\sigma=\\sigma,\\qquad \\sigma\\times\\sigma=1+\\psi.
\\\]]{.math .display}

In the first relation, [\\(a\\)]{.math .inline} denotes any of the three
charge labels. Fusion with the vacuum charge leaves a charge unchanged.

The relation [\\(\\psi\\times\\psi=1\\)]{.math .inline} states that two
[\\(\\psi\\)]{.math .inline} charges have vacuum total charge. The
relation [\\(\\psi\\times\\sigma=\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline} states that
combining [\\(\\psi\\)]{.math .inline} with [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math
.inline} gives total charge [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline}.

The final relation gives two [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline} charges a
choice of total charge: [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline} or [\\(\\psi\\)]{.math
.inline}.

The same fusion rules can be represented as a table in which each entry
lists the allowed total charges:

::: {.table-scroll aria-label="Ising fusion table" role="region" tabindex="0"}
  [\\(\\times\\)]{.math .inline}   [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline}         [\\(\\psi\\)]{.math .inline}     [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline}
  -------------------------------- -------------------------------- -------------------------------- --------------------------------
  [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline}         [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline}         [\\(\\psi\\)]{.math .inline}     [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline}
  [\\(\\psi\\)]{.math .inline}     [\\(\\psi\\)]{.math .inline}     [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline}         [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline}
  [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline}   [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline}   [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline}   [\\(1+\\psi\\)]{.math .inline}
:::

Every nonempty entry in this table contains one total charge except the
final entry. Each allowed total occurs with coefficient one.

The integer multiplying a total charge, conventionally omitted when it
equals one, is the fusion coefficient. It counts independent fusion
states and is not a probability.

All nonzero fusion coefficients in the Ising model equal one. The model
is therefore multiplicity-free, meaning that each allowed total has
exactly one fusion channel and each forbidden total has none.

The vector space of ways in which charges [\\(a\\)]{.math .inline} and
[\\(b\\)]{.math .inline} can have total charge [\\(c\\)]{.math .inline}
is denoted by

[\\\[ V\_{ab}\^{c},\\qquad \\dim V\_{ab}\^{c}=N\_{ab}\^{c}. \\\]]{.math
.display}

This space is called a fusion space, and its dimension equals the
corresponding fusion coefficient. For two [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline}
charges, [\\(V\_{\\sigma\\sigma}\^{1}\\)]{.math .inline} and
[\\(V\_{\\sigma\\sigma}\^{\\psi}\\)]{.math .inline} are each
one-dimensional, whereas [\\(V\_{\\sigma\\sigma}\^{\\sigma}\\)]{.math
.inline} is zero-dimensional and therefore represents a forbidden
channel.

If one were instead to propose
[\\(N\_{\\sigma\\sigma}\^{\\sigma}=1\\)]{.math .inline}, two
[\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline} charges would also be allowed to have
total charge [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline}. The resulting fusion table
would not be the Ising table. The absence of this channel is part of the
defining fusion data.
::::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Diagrammatic representation of a fusion vertex

A basis vector in [\\(V\_{ab}\^{c}\\)]{.math .inline} can be represented
by a trivalent vertex, meaning a vertex with three incident edges.
Diagrams in this chapter are read from top to bottom: the incoming
charges enter at the top, and their total charge exits at the bottom.

    a   b
     \ /
      |
      c

When [\\(N\_{ab}\^{c}\>1\\)]{.math .inline}, a multiplicity label
[\\(\\mu=1,\\ldots,N\_{ab}\^{c}\\)]{.math .inline} must be placed beside
the vertex. The fusion channel is then specified by the complete tuple
[\\((a,b;c,\\mu)\\)]{.math .inline}, rather than by [\\(c\\)]{.math
.inline} alone.

Three or more charges must be represented using a sequence of pairwise
fusion operations. Such a diagram is called a fusion tree.

The internal edges of a fusion tree carry intermediate charges.
Selecting the labels on these edges, together with any required
multiplicity labels, selects a basis state.

A fusion tree organizes a many-particle state by groupings, recording
which pair fuses first in the bookkeeping. That ordering carries no
claim that the system underwent a literal temporal sequence of
collisions.

If multiplicity labels are omitted when [\\(N\_{ab}\^{c}\>1\\)]{.math
.inline}, multiple independent states with the same total charge are
incorrectly represented as a single vector. The statement that an
internal-edge label specifies the state is valid only when every
relevant fusion coefficient is zero or one.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Three-particle fusion bases

Consider three Ising [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline} charges constrained
to have total charge [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline}. In the
left-associated basis, the left pair is fused first. Its intermediate
charge [\\(x\\)]{.math .inline} can be [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline} or
[\\(\\psi\\)]{.math .inline}, and either intermediate result can then
fuse with the third [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline} to produce total
charge [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline}:

    Left pairing:  ((σ σ)_x σ)_σ

    σ   σ   σ
     \ /    |
      x     |
       \   /
        \ /
         σ

    x = 1 or ψ

Alternatively, the right pair can be fused first. Its intermediate
charge [\\(y\\)]{.math .inline} can likewise be [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline}
or [\\(\\psi\\)]{.math .inline}:

    Right pairing:  (σ (σ σ)_y)_σ

    σ   σ   σ
    |    \ /
    |     y
     \   /
      \ /
       σ

    y = 1 or ψ

These two trees share external charges and total charge. They define two
bases of one vector space: the three-particle fusion space, which is the
state space on which the braid operations of the previous chapter act.

The dimension follows directly from the fusion table. In the left
pairing, the first pair can have total charge [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline}
or [\\(\\psi\\)]{.math .inline}, and either intermediate charge can fuse
with the remaining [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline} to give total charge
[\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline}.

The left pairing therefore contains two states, and the right pairing
describes the same two-dimensional space in a different basis. Three
[\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline} charges constrained to total charge
[\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline} thus support a two-dimensional fusion
space; changing the total-charge constraint generally changes the space.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### The [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-move as a change of fusion basis

The following diagram represents a change of pairing rather than motion
of the particles:

    σ   σ   σ               σ   σ   σ
     \ /    |               |    \ /
      x     |     -->       |     y
       \   /                 \   /
        \ /                   \ /
         σ                     σ

This change of pairing is called an [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-move. A
distinct operation introduced later, the [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-move,
exchanges particle positions.

Let [\\(\|x\\rangle_L\\)]{.math .inline} denote orthonormal states in
the left-pairing basis, and let [\\(\|y\\rangle_R\\)]{.math .inline}
denote orthonormal states in the right-pairing basis. The
[\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-move is the basis transformation

[\\\[ \|x\\rangle_L=\\sum\_{y\\in\\{1,\\psi\\}}
\\left\[F\^{\\sigma\\sigma\\sigma}\_{\\sigma}\\right\]\_{xy}\|y\\rangle_R.
\\\]]{.math .display}

In a standard gauge for Ising anyons,

[\\\[ F\^{\\sigma\\sigma\\sigma}\_{\\sigma} =\\frac{1}{\\sqrt 2}
\\begin{pmatrix} 1&1\\\\ 1&-1 \\end{pmatrix}, \\\]]{.math .display}

where the rows correspond to [\\(x=(1,\\psi)\\)]{.math .inline} and the
columns correspond to [\\(y=(1,\\psi)\\)]{.math .inline}
[\[R015\]](#ref-R015 "[R015] C. Nayak, S. H. Simon, A. Stern, M. Freedman, and S. Das
Sarma, “Non-Abelian Anyons and Topological Quantum Computation,” Reviews
of Modern Physics 80, 1083–1159 (2008). DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.80.1083 ;
arXiv: 0707.1889 ."){.citation};
[\[R023\]](#ref-R023 "[R023] P. Bonderson, K. Shtengel, and J. K. Slingerland,
“Interferometry of Non-Abelian Anyons,” Annals of Physics 323, 2709–2755
(2008). DOI: 10.1016/j.aop.2008.01.012 ;
arXiv: 0707.4206 ."){.citation}. Here a gauge is a choice of phases for
the basis vectors at fusion vertices. The explicit basis transformation
is

[\\\[ \|1\\rangle_L=\\frac{\|1\\rangle_R+\|\\psi\\rangle_R}{\\sqrt2},
\\qquad
\|\\psi\\rangle_L=\\frac{\|1\\rangle_R-\|\\psi\\rangle_R}{\\sqrt2}.
\\\]]{.math .display}

Suppose the first two charges are prepared with definite fusion channel
[\\(x=1\\)]{.math .inline}. If the last two charges are measured
instead, the amplitudes are [\\(1/\\sqrt2\\)]{.math .inline} for
[\\(y=1\\)]{.math .inline} and [\\(1/\\sqrt2\\)]{.math .inline} for
[\\(y=\\psi\\)]{.math .inline}.

By the Born rule, which assigns a measurement probability equal to the
squared magnitude of the corresponding amplitude, each result has
probability [\\(1/2\\)]{.math .inline}. These probabilities are
determined by the [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-matrix, while the fusion
table lists only the available channels.

The amplitudes satisfy the normalization condition

[\\\[ \\left\|\\frac{1}{\\sqrt2}\\right\|\^2+
\\left\|\\frac{1}{\\sqrt2}\\right\|\^2=1. \\\]]{.math .display}

In addition, [\\(F\^\\dagger F=I\\)]{.math .inline}, where
[\\(F\^\\dagger\\)]{.math .inline} is the conjugate transpose and
[\\(I\\)]{.math .inline} is the [\\(2\\times2\\)]{.math .inline}
identity matrix. Thus, changing the pairing preserves inner products and
measurement probabilities.

An [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-move is therefore a unitary change of basis
within a fixed fusion space, leaving particle positions in place.

If [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline} were not unitary, inner products and
therefore Born probabilities would depend on which pairing served to
represent the state, and the two fusion trees could not both count as
bases of one physical state space.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Antiparticles and the vacuum channel

Each simple charge [\\(a\\)]{.math .inline}, where a simple charge is an
irreducible charge type, has a partner [\\(\\bar a\\)]{.math .inline}
such that their fusion contains the vacuum channel:

[\\\[ N\_{a\\bar a}\^{1}\\ge 1. \\\]]{.math .display}

The charge [\\(\\bar a\\)]{.math .inline} is called the antiparticle of
[\\(a\\)]{.math .inline}. The pair can fuse to vacuum, analogous to the
disappearance of a particle-antiparticle pair into the vacuum sector.

In the common simple setting, the vacuum channel occurs exactly once. A
charge can be its own antiparticle. In the Ising fusion table,
[\\(\\bar\\sigma=\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline} and
[\\(\\bar\\psi=\\psi\\)]{.math .inline}.

A physical fusion experiment can give probabilistic outcomes while every
fusion coefficient [\\(N\_{ab}\^{c}\\)]{.math .inline} is zero or one,
because a coefficient counts basis states and the prepared state
supplies the amplitudes. The value [\\(N\_{ab}\^{c}=2\\)]{.math .inline}
instead means two orthogonal states sharing the external labels
[\\(a,b,c\\)]{.math .inline}, so a multiplicity label must join the
description before amplitudes enter.

Every charge needs its antiparticle partner: with no [\\(\\bar
a\\)]{.math .inline}, charge [\\(a\\)]{.math .inline} would have no
fusion path to vacuum, leaving the vacuum sector unreachable from that
charge and the theory without duals in the sense used later.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Associativity and dimension counting

Three charges can be grouped two ways --- fuse the first pair first, or
the last pair first --- and both must describe the same space of states.
Counting that space each way gives a consistency check on the fusion
coefficients, before any phases or matrices enter. Written out, fixing
the total charge [\\(d\\)]{.math .inline}, the left-associated
(first-pair-first) fusion space decomposes as

[\\\[ V\_{abc}\^{d}\\cong \\bigoplus_e V\_{ab}\^{e}\\otimes
V\_{ec}\^{d}. \\\]]{.math .display}

Here [\\(e\\)]{.math .inline} ranges over allowed intermediate charges,
[\\(\\oplus\\)]{.math .inline} denotes a direct sum over alternative
intermediate sectors, and [\\(\\otimes\\)]{.math .inline} combines the
two vertex spaces along a selected fusion path. The same fusion space
has the right-associated decomposition

[\\\[ V\_{abc}\^{d}\\cong \\bigoplus_f V\_{bc}\^{f}\\otimes
V\_{af}\^{d}. \\\]]{.math .display}

Because these are two decompositions of the same vector space, their
dimensions must agree. This requirement gives an integer consistency
condition on the fusion table before any phases are assigned:

[\\\[ \\sum_e N\_{ab}\^{e}N\_{ec}\^{d} = \\sum_f
N\_{bc}\^{f}N\_{af}\^{d}. \\\]]{.math .display}

Coefficients violating this equation admit no phase assignment that
renders the fusion rules associative.

For three [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline} charges with total charge
[\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline}, the left-associated dimension is

[\\\[ N\_{\\sigma\\sigma}\^{1}N\_{1\\sigma}\^{\\sigma} +
N\_{\\sigma\\sigma}\^{\\psi}N\_{\\psi\\sigma}\^{\\sigma} +
N\_{\\sigma\\sigma}\^{\\sigma}N\_{\\sigma\\sigma}\^{\\sigma} =
(1)(1)+(1)(1)+(0)(0) =2. \\\]]{.math .display}

The right-associated calculation is the same sum with the first pair
replaced by the last pair, and it also equals [\\(2\\)]{.math .inline}.
The Ising fusion table therefore passes this consistency test.

For [\\(n\\)]{.math .inline} charges, the construction is repeated.
External edges record the [\\(n\\)]{.math .inline} individual charges,
internal edges record intermediate charges, and the root records the
total charge. The number of admissible edge labelings, including vertex
multiplicities, equals the dimension of the fusion space with fixed
total charge.

This multiplicity of internal labelings explains how non-Abelian charges
can store information. Even when the total charge is fixed, several
distinct internal fusion states can remain.

A local measurement enclosing only one separated particle cannot
determine the complete internal fusion pattern. \[Theory\] In an ideal
topological phase, operations supported far from one another act on this
nonlocal fusion space according to the theory's data, up to corrections
caused by finite separation and unwanted excitations
[\[R015\]](#ref-R015 "[R015] C. Nayak, S. H. Simon, A. Stern, M. Freedman, and S. Das
Sarma, “Non-Abelian Anyons and Topological Quantum Computation,” Reviews
of Modern Physics 80, 1083–1159 (2008). DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.80.1083 ;
arXiv: 0707.1889 ."){.citation};
[\[R017\]](#ref-R017 "[R017] A. Kitaev, “Anyons in an Exactly Solved Model and Beyond,”
Annals of Physics 321, 2–111 (2006). DOI: 10.1016/j.aop.2005.10.005 ;
arXiv: cond-mat/0506438 ."){.citation}.

This identity belongs to the effective theory; a fabricated device needs
separate experimental confirmation. Associativity of fusion therefore
imposes a numerical identity on the fusion coefficients at the level of
dimensions, and a failing identity leaves no consistent three-charge
fusion space.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Quantum dimensions and fusion-space growth

The quantum dimension [\\(d_a\\)]{.math .inline} measures the asymptotic
contribution of charge [\\(a\\)]{.math .inline} to the growth of large
fusion spaces. For a unitary theory, the quantum dimensions are chosen
as positive numbers satisfying

[\\\[ d_a d_b=\\sum_c N\_{ab}\^{c}d_c, \\qquad d_1=1. \\\]]{.math
.display}

Equivalently, define the fusion matrix
[\\((N_a)\^c{}\_{b}=N\_{ab}\^{c}\\)]{.math .inline}. Then
[\\(d_a\\)]{.math .inline} is its largest positive eigenvalue in the
relevant sector. This follows from the Perron--Frobenius theorem and is
not a fitted parameter
[\[R017\]](#ref-R017 "[R017] A. Kitaev, “Anyons in an Exactly Solved Model and Beyond,”
Annals of Physics 321, 2–111 (2006). DOI: 10.1016/j.aop.2005.10.005 ;
arXiv: cond-mat/0506438 ."){.citation};
[\[R016\]](#ref-R016 "[R016] E. C. Rowell and Z. Wang, “Mathematics of Topological
Quantum Computing,” Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 55,
183–238 (2018). DOI: 10.1090/bull/1605 ; arXiv: 1705.06206 ."){.citation}.

Applying these relations to the Ising fusion table,
[\\(\\psi\\times\\psi=1\\)]{.math .inline} gives
[\\(d\_\\psi\^2=1\\)]{.math .inline}. Positivity therefore requires
[\\(d\_\\psi=1\\)]{.math .inline}. Similarly,
[\\(\\sigma\\times\\sigma=1+\\psi\\)]{.math .inline} gives

[\\\[ d\_\\sigma\^2=d_1+d\_\\psi=2, \\qquad d\_\\sigma=\\sqrt2.
\\\]]{.math .display}

The value [\\(\\sqrt2\\)]{.math .inline} cannot count states in an
ordinary local vector space, whose dimensions are integers.

Instead, [\\(d\_\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline} characterizes asymptotic
growth. For [\\(2n\\)]{.math .inline} Ising [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math
.inline} charges constrained to have total charge [\\(1\\)]{.math
.inline}, the fusion-space dimension is [\\(2\^{n-1}\\)]{.math .inline}:
two charges give one state, four give two, six give four, and the
pattern continues.

The characteristic multiplicative contribution associated with each
additional [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline} approaches
[\\(\\sqrt2\\)]{.math .inline}.

In a unitary fusion theory, a charge with [\\(d_a=1\\)]{.math .inline}
is Abelian. A charge with [\\(d_a\>1\\)]{.math .inline} supports
non-Abelian growth of its fusion spaces. The total quantum dimension is

[\\\[ \\mathcal D=\\sqrt{\\sum_a d_a\^2}, \\\]]{.math .display}

where the sum extends over all simple charges. For the Ising theory,
[\\(\\mathcal D=\\sqrt{1+1+2}=2\\)]{.math .inline}.

Thus [\\(d\_\\sigma=\\sqrt2\\)]{.math .inline} reads as an asymptotic
growth rate, not as a count of local on-site levels: local Hilbert-space
dimensions take integer values.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### General [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-moves with fusion multiplicities

The simple [\\(2\\times2\\)]{.math .inline} [\\(F\\)]{.math
.inline}-matrix above already covers every theory in this book, because
Ising and Fibonacci are both multiplicity-free (each fusion coefficient
is [\\(0\\)]{.math .inline} or [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline}). The general
form below is needed only when some [\\(N\_{ab}\^{c}\>1\\)]{.math
.inline}, so a vertex carries an extra label; a reader focused on Ising
or Fibonacci can skip to the next section.

Let [\\(a,b,c\\)]{.math .inline} be three incoming charges with total
charge [\\(d\\)]{.math .inline}. In the left-associated tree, let
[\\(e\\)]{.math .inline} denote the intermediate charge, let
[\\(\\mu\\)]{.math .inline} label a basis of [\\(V\_{ab}\^{e}\\)]{.math
.inline}, and let [\\(\\nu\\)]{.math .inline} label a basis of
[\\(V\_{ec}\^{d}\\)]{.math .inline}. In the right-associated tree, let
[\\(f\\)]{.math .inline}, [\\(\\alpha\\)]{.math .inline}, and
[\\(\\beta\\)]{.math .inline} denote the corresponding intermediate
charge and multiplicity labels. The general basis transformation is

[\\\[ \\big\|((ab)\_e c)\_d;\\mu,\\nu\\big\\rangle =
\\sum\_{f,\\alpha,\\beta}
\\left\[F\^{abc}\_{d}\\right\]\_{(e,\\mu,\\nu)(f,\\alpha,\\beta)}
\\big\|(a(bc)\_f)\_d;\\alpha,\\beta\\big\\rangle. \\\]]{.math .display}

This equation defines the [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-matrix convention
used in this chapter. Other sources may use the inverse transformation,
take a complex conjugate, or arrange the labels differently. Such
alternatives are equivalent provided that the convention is stated and
applied consistently.

An [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-move remains a change of basis and does not
exchange particle positions. Its individual matrix entries depend on the
phase choices assigned to the vertex basis states.

These phase choices constitute a gauge. Observable probabilities and
complete braid amplitudes are gauge-independent.

Rephasing a vertex basis changes the individual [\\(F\\)]{.math
.inline}-symbols. It does not change closed-process probabilities,
consistency relations, or physically defined interference signals. An
individual gauge-dependent matrix entry is therefore not itself an
observable.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### The [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-move as particle exchange

An [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-move exchanges two neighboring particles.
For a counterclockwise exchange of charges [\\(a\\)]{.math .inline} and
[\\(b\\)]{.math .inline} in total channel [\\(c\\)]{.math .inline}, it
is the unitary map

[\\\[ R\^{ab}\_{c}:V\_{ab}\^{c}\\longrightarrow V\_{ba}\^{c}.
\\\]]{.math .display}

Diagrammatically, an [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-move contains a crossing
rather than a change of pairing:

    a   b               b   a
     \ /       -->       \ /
      c                   c

The [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-move represents an actual braid and is
distinct from an [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-move.

In a multiplicity-free theory, each allowed [\\(R\^{ab}\_{c}\\)]{.math
.inline} is a phase. In the same standard Ising gauge used above,

[\\\[ R\^{\\sigma\\sigma}\_{1}=e\^{-i\\pi/8}, \\qquad
R\^{\\sigma\\sigma}\_{\\psi}=e\^{3i\\pi/8} \\\]]{.math .display}

for a chosen counterclockwise convention
[\[R015\]](#ref-R015 "[R015] C. Nayak, S. H. Simon, A. Stern, M. Freedman, and S. Das
Sarma, “Non-Abelian Anyons and Topological Quantum Computation,” Reviews
of Modern Physics 80, 1083–1159 (2008). DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.80.1083 ;
arXiv: 0707.1889 ."){.citation};
[\[R023\]](#ref-R023 "[R023] P. Bonderson, K. Shtengel, and J. K. Slingerland,
“Interferometry of Non-Abelian Anyons,” Annals of Physics 323, 2709–2755
(2008). DOI: 10.1016/j.aop.2008.01.012 ;
arXiv: 0707.4206 ."){.citation}. Reversing the direction of exchange
applies the inverse phases.

In the left-pairing basis of three [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline}
charges, exchanging the first two particles is represented by the
diagonal matrix

[\\\[ B\_{12}= \\begin{pmatrix} R\^{\\sigma\\sigma}\_{1}&0\\\\
0&R\^{\\sigma\\sigma}\_{\\psi} \\end{pmatrix}. \\\]]{.math .display}

To exchange the last two particles, the state is first transformed into
the basis in which those particles fuse directly. Their [\\(R\\)]{.math
.inline}-move is then applied, followed by the inverse basis
transformation:

[\\\[ B\_{23}=F\\,B\_{12}\\,F\^{-1} \\\]]{.math .display}

for the matrix convention used in the worked example. Because
[\\(F\\)]{.math .inline} mixes the two fusion channels and the two
[\\(R\\)]{.math .inline} phases are different, [\\(B\_{12}\\)]{.math
.inline} and [\\(B\_{23}\\)]{.math .inline} do not commute. This
provides the explicit mechanism for a non-Abelian braid action.

A braid involving particles that are not adjacent fusion partners
generally requires both operations: [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline} regroups
the fusion tree to bring the pair together, and [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}
then performs the exchange. Regrouping alone performs no exchange.

Equal [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline} phases would collapse both
[\\(B\_{12}\\)]{.math .inline} and [\\(B\_{23}\\)]{.math .inline} to the
same global phase, so the two operations would commute and the
non-Abelian action on this two-dimensional fusion space would disappear
with the fusion table unchanged.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Coherence conditions for fusion and braiding data

Four charges can be regrouped through different sequences of
[\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-moves. When two sequences begin and end with
the same fusion trees, they must define the same linear map.

This consistency requirement is the pentagon equation. Similarly, two
equivalent sequences of regrouping and exchanging three charges lead to
the hexagon equations, which constrain [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline} and
[\\(R\\)]{.math .inline} jointly.

These coherence equations ensure that a complicated diagram has a unique
value independent of the intermediate bookkeeping choices
[\[R022\]](#ref-R022 "[R022] G. Moore and N. Seiberg, “Classical and Quantum Conformal
Field Theory,” Communications in Mathematical Physics 123, 177–254
(1989). DOI: 10.1007/BF01238857 ."){.citation}.

At this point you have the complete computational data: the fusion table
[\\(N\_{ab}\^{c}\\)]{.math .inline}, the [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-moves,
and the [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-moves. The mathematical literature
bundles that package under one name, the *fusion category*, developed in
full in Appendix D. The vocabulary adds no new operations; each term
simply renames an object already in hand:

- **Simple objects** --- the charge types. **Tensor product** ---
  fusion. **Unit object** --- the vacuum [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline}.
  **Associator** --- the [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-matrices.
  (*Semisimple* just means every object is a finite direct sum of charge
  types.)

- **Dual objects** --- antiparticles.

- **Braided fusion category** --- a fusion category with exchange data
  added, that is, the [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-moves. Braiding is
  optional: without it there are no [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-moves.

- **Unitary modular tensor category** --- the above with unitarity and a
  nondegeneracy condition on braiding: the standard structure for a
  complete two-dimensional anyon theory
  [\[R017\]](#ref-R017 "[R017] A. Kitaev, “Anyons in an Exactly Solved Model and Beyond,”
  Annals of Physics 321, 2–111 (2006). DOI: 10.1016/j.aop.2005.10.005 ;
  arXiv: cond-mat/0506438 ."){.citation};
  [\[R016\]](#ref-R016 "[R016] E. C. Rowell and Z. Wang, “Mathematics of Topological
  Quantum Computing,” Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 55,
  183–238 (2018). DOI: 10.1090/bull/1605 ; arXiv: 1705.06206 ."){.citation}.

The same fusion coefficients [\\(N\_{ab}\^{c}\\)]{.math .inline} can
admit inequivalent but internally consistent choices of [\\(F\\)]{.math
.inline}- and [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-data. Fusion rules are necessary
input but do not uniquely characterize the theory
[\[R016\]](#ref-R016 "[R016] E. C. Rowell and Z. Wang, “Mathematics of Topological
Quantum Computing,” Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 55,
183–238 (2018). DOI: 10.1090/bull/1605 ; arXiv: 1705.06206 ."){.citation}.
If the pentagon or hexagon equations fail, a larger diagram does not
have a well-defined value because different evaluation routes give
different results.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Operational evidence in laboratory systems

The preceding symbols define an effective theory. A laboratory system
instead consists of a finite sample, control mechanisms, detectors,
unwanted excitations, boundaries, and a microscopic Hamiltonian.
Fusion-category data are therefore inferred from measurements rather
than read directly from a dedicated instrument.

\[Experiment\] Evidence for fusion data must be based on operationally
distinguishable outcomes. Relevant procedures include creating or
identifying excitations, combining spatial regions, measuring total
charge, and showing that the observed channels agree with a consistent
fusion rule. Interferometry provides one possible method for measuring
charge because a probe can respond to the monodromy of the enclosed
charge, where monodromy is the effect produced by winding the probe
around that charge
[\[R023\]](#ref-R023 "[R023] P. Bonderson, K. Shtengel, and J. K. Slingerland,
“Interferometry of Non-Abelian Anyons,” Annals of Physics 323, 2709–2755
(2008). DOI: 10.1016/j.aop.2008.01.012 ;
arXiv: 0707.4206 ."){.citation}. A single spectral peak or degeneracy is
insufficient to reconstruct [\\(N\\)]{.math .inline}, and still less
sufficient to determine [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline} and [\\(R\\)]{.math
.inline}.

\[Experiment\] Evidence for an [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-matrix requires
comparison of incompatible fusion-tree measurements while maintaining
enough phase coherence to recover amplitudes rather than only the set of
allowed outcomes. Evidence for [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline} requires
controlled exchanges, or an operationally equivalent braid, together
with measurements of channel-dependent phases. Multiple operation
sequences should satisfy the braid and coherence relations within the
measured uncertainty.

\[Theory\] Even exact agreement with a limited set of matrices
establishes the effective operations tested, and those alone. A claim of
emergent anyons additionally requires excitations arising from a
many-body phase, deconfinement over the relevant length scale, and data
stable under allowed local perturbations.

A claim of topological protection must also bound errors from
non-topological processes, thermal excitation, finite-size splitting,
and control faults. These are physical requirements beyond the fusion
and braiding algebra
[\[R015\]](#ref-R015 "[R015] C. Nayak, S. H. Simon, A. Stern, M. Freedman, and S. Das
Sarma, “Non-Abelian Anyons and Topological Quantum Computation,” Reviews
of Modern Physics 80, 1083–1159 (2008). DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.80.1083 ;
arXiv: 0707.1889 ."){.citation};
[\[R017\]](#ref-R017 "[R017] A. Kitaev, “Anyons in an Exactly Solved Model and Beyond,”
Annals of Physics 321, 2–111 (2006). DOI: 10.1016/j.aop.2005.10.005 ;
arXiv: cond-mat/0506438 ."){.citation}.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Digital emulation, defects, and emergent anyons

A digital processor can encode the two Ising fusion-tree basis states in
ordinary qubits and implement the Hadamard matrix displayed above. Such
an implementation is a digital emulation of an [\\(F\\)]{.math
.inline}-move.

A collection of defect spins can similarly encode a two-dimensional
subspace. Both constructions operate on ordinary local degrees of
freedom; emergent [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline} anyons and topological
order need the many-body phase evidence described above.

Extrinsic defects can carry nontrivial projective fusion and braiding
properties, but they must be distinguished from intrinsic quasiparticles
that propagate freely within the host phase
[\[R021\]](#ref-R021 "[R021] M. Barkeshli, P. Bonderson, M. Cheng, and Z. Wang,
“Symmetry Fractionalization, Defects, and Gauging of Topological
Phases,” Physical Review B 100, 115147 (2019). DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevB.100.115147 ;
arXiv: 1410.4540 ."){.citation}. The same algebra can occur in several
physical settings, and experimental evidence from the hardware
determines which setting is realized.

Assigning anyonic labels to defect-spin energy levels leaves the
physical claim unestablished until the proposed microscopic Hamiltonian
is shown to generate emergent excitations whose low-energy states obey
consistent fusion and braiding data; later chapters examine whether this
more demanding physical requirement is plausible.

A programmed braid and an emergent anyon therefore remain distinct
claims when the relevant algebra concerns fusion rather than exchange.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Common conceptual errors

- Interpreting "[\\(+\\)]{.math .inline}" as a prepared quantum
  superposition is incorrect. In a fusion rule, "[\\(+\\)]{.math
  .inline}" denotes the allowed total-charge sectors. A quantum state,
  including its amplitudes in those sectors, can be specified only with
  additional preparation information.

- Interpreting [\\(N\_{ab}\^{c}\\)]{.math .inline} as a probability is
  incorrect. The fusion multiplicity [\\(N\_{ab}\^{c}\\)]{.math .inline}
  is the integer dimension of the space of fusion channels in which
  charges [\\(a\\)]{.math .inline} and [\\(b\\)]{.math .inline} combine
  to total charge [\\(c\\)]{.math .inline}. Probabilities instead follow
  from normalized state amplitudes together with a specified measurement
  protocol.

- Interpreting quantum dimension as the number of states at a single
  site is incorrect. Quantum dimension characterizes the asymptotic
  growth of fusion-space dimension as the number of charges increases.
  Thus, [\\(d\_\\sigma=\\sqrt2\\)]{.math .inline} cannot be the
  dimension of a finite local vector space.

- Not every basis transformation is a braid. An [\\(F\\)]{.math
  .inline}-move changes the grouping, or parenthesization, of a fusion
  tree without exchanging the spatial positions of charges. An
  [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-move exchanges two charges. Braiding
  nonadjacent fusion partners generally requires both [\\(F\\)]{.math
  .inline}- and [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-moves.

- The total-charge constraint cannot be omitted. Three
  [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline} charges constrained to have total
  charge [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline} form the two-dimensional example
  discussed above. A different total-charge constraint generally
  produces a different fusion space.

- Multiplicity labels cannot be omitted in a general theory. The
  statement that an internal-edge label completely specifies a
  fusion-tree basis state is valid only when all relevant fusion
  multiplicities satisfy [\\(N\_{ab}\^{c}\\le1\\)]{.math .inline}. If a
  fusion vertex has multiplicity greater than one, an additional vertex
  label is required to distinguish the independent fusion channels.

- Gauge-dependent matrix entries are not themselves observables. Here, a
  gauge choice is a choice of basis phases at fusion vertices. Rephasing
  such a vertex basis changes individual [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}- and
  [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-symbols, which are the matrix elements
  associated with reassociation and exchange operations. By contrast,
  probabilities for closed processes, consistency relations, and
  physically defined interference signals are gauge invariant, meaning
  that they do not depend on this basis choice.

- Fusion rules do not uniquely determine a topological phase. The same
  fusion coefficients [\\(N\_{ab}\^{c}\\)]{.math .inline} can admit
  inequivalent sets of consistent [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}- and
  [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-data. Fusion rules are therefore necessary
  input, but they are not a complete specification of the phase
  [\[R016\]](#ref-R016 "[R016] E. C. Rowell and Z. Wang, “Mathematics of Topological
  Quantum Computing,” Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 55,
  183–238 (2018). DOI: 10.1090/bull/1605 ; arXiv: 1705.06206 ."){.citation}.

- Labels used in a simulator must not be identified automatically with
  material excitations. A quantum circuit can reproduce fusion-space
  algebra accurately even when every underlying carrier is an ordinary
  physical qubit, meaning a physical two-level quantum system. Such a
  construction is a simulation rather than, by itself, evidence for
  emergent material excitations.

- Algebraic data do not establish the existence of a microscopic energy
  gap. A consistent set of [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}- and [\\(R\\)]{.math
  .inline}-tables does not prove that a proposed defect Hamiltonian
  realizes those data. Such a realization additionally requires a gapped
  many-body phase, appropriate excitations, and stability under
  realistic perturbations.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Verification exercises

- The equation [\\(N\_{ab}\^{c}=2\\)]{.math .inline} states that there
  are two linearly independent fusion channels in which charges
  [\\(a\\)]{.math .inline} and [\\(b\\)]{.math .inline} combine to total
  charge [\\(c\\)]{.math .inline}. A multiplicity label is therefore
  required to distinguish them.

- Both pairings of three Ising [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline} charges
  with total charge [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline} have dimension two.
  For the left pairing, [\\\[
  N\_{\\sigma\\sigma}\^{1}N\_{1\\sigma}\^{\\sigma}+N\_{\\sigma\\sigma}\^{\\psi}N\_{\\psi\\sigma}\^{\\sigma}=1+1=2.
  \\\]]{.math .display} The right pairing gives the same sum when it is
  applied to the last pair. The two fusion trees therefore provide two
  different bases for the same two-dimensional fusion space.

- A fusion tree records the organization of successive fusion
  operations. Its external edges specify the initial charges, its
  internal edges specify intermediate charges, its vertices may carry
  multiplicity labels, and its root specifies the total charge.

- If [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline} were not unitary, inner products would
  depend on the pairing used to represent the state. A unitary
  transformation preserves inner products, so failure of unitarity would
  cause Born probabilities---the probabilities obtained from squared
  state amplitudes---for the same physical question to disagree between
  pairings.

- An [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-move changes the pairing of charges
  without exchanging their positions. An [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-move
  exchanges neighboring charges within a specified fusion channel.

- Reproducing an [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-matrix with defect-spin qubits
  demonstrates an encoded operation. Emergent anyons need independent
  evidence for both a many-body topological phase and its emergent
  excitations.

Fusion rules list the allowed outcomes, an [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-move
regroups three charges, and an [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-move exchanges
two charges. The next analysis applies this machinery to a single
nontrivial charge [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}, whose fusion-space
dimensions generate the Fibonacci numbers.
:::

  Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 55, 183--238 (2018).
  DOI: [10.1090/bull/1605](https://doi.org/10.1090/bull/1605);
  [arXiv:1705.06206](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.06206).

:::: {.section .book-part aria-labelledby="part-vii-fibonacci-anyons"}
## Part VII --- Fibonacci anyons

::: {.chapter-intro math-section=""}
The preceding chapter introduced fusion rules, which specify the
possible outcomes when topological charges combine. Here we study the
Fibonacci fusion rule in detail.

**In the arc:** Stage 03 · COLLECTIVE: the specific anyon theory the
architecture aims for.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
:::
::::

## Chapter 15 --- Two fusion outcomes for a pair of Fibonacci anyons

::: {.chapter-intro math-section=""}
Consider a topological charge denoted by [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}.
When two such charges are combined, their total charge can be either the
vacuum or another [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}:

[\\\[ \\tau\\times\\tau=1+\\tau. \\\]]{.math .display}

This equation defines the Fibonacci fusion rule. The symbol
[\\(1\\)]{.math .inline} denotes the vacuum charge, so the vacuum
outcome means that the two [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} charges can
annihilate.

The plus sign lists alternative fusion outcomes; unlike ordinary
addition, it records that a measurement of the pair's total charge
returns [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline} or [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}, with
one outcome realized per measurement.

**Assumes:** Chapter 14 --- fusion rules, fusion spaces and trees, and
the [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}- and [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-moves.
**Introduces:** the single Fibonacci rule
[\\(\\tau\\times\\tau=1+\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}, the Fibonacci growth
of fusion-space dimension and the golden-ratio quantum dimension, the
three-anyon qubit and its braid matrices, and why braiding these anyons
is computationally universal. **Used later in:** string nets (Chapter
18), chirality (Chapter 19), and the defect-array architecture (Chapter
24). **Watch:** this is one specific anyon theory instantiating Chapter
14\'s general framework --- the [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}- and
[\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-symbols here are particular numbers, not new
definitions.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Self-duality and fusion channels

This theory contains only two topological-charge labels: the vacuum
[\\(1\\)]{.math .inline} and the nontrivial charge [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math
.inline}.

The vacuum is the identity element of fusion. For either charge
[\\(a\\)]{.math .inline},

[\\\[ 1\\times a=a\\times1=a. \\\]]{.math .display}

A single [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} therefore retains charge
[\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}. The only fusion process with multiple
possible outcomes is the fusion of two [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}
charges.

The charge [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} is its own antiparticle: fusing
it with another [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} can produce vacuum, which
is the defining property called self-duality. Thus [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math
.inline} is self-dual, and self-duality places the vacuum outcome in
[\\(\\tau\\times\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}, as the rule shows.

The two terms on the right-hand side identify two orthogonal fusion
outcomes, called fusion channels --- the terminology introduced for
Ising anyons in the previous chapter --- rather than pieces of divided
particles. In the Fibonacci theory, the channels of
[\\(\\tau\\times\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} are exactly [\\(1\\)]{.math
.inline} and [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}.
:::

:::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Counting fusion histories

For an ordered collection of [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} charges,
sequential fusion defines an intermediate total charge that can be
either [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline} or [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}. Adding
one more [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} produces the following
transitions. A previous total charge [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline} must
become [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}, because
[\\(1\\times\\tau=\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}. A previous total charge
[\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} can become either [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline}
or [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}, because
[\\(\\tau\\times\\tau=1+\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}.

``` text
old total add τ new total
1 ------> τ
τ ------> 1 or τ
```

A valid sequence of intermediate charge labels, called a fusion history,
specifies one basis state of the many-particle fusion space. Each added
[\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} charge opens further histories, so their
number grows with the collection size.

Let [\\(A_n\\)]{.math .inline} denote the number of fusion histories for
[\\(n\\)]{.math .inline} copies of [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} with
total charge [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline}. Let [\\(B_n\\)]{.math .inline}
denote the number with total charge [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}. Adding
another [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} gives

[\\\[ A\_{n+1}=B_n, \\qquad B\_{n+1}=A_n+B_n. \\\]]{.math .display}

The first equation counts the single route to vacuum: only a previous
total charge [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} combines with the new
[\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} to produce [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline}. The
second equation counts both routes to [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}: from
a previous [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline} or a previous [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math
.inline}. The fusion rule and the initial conditions therefore fix both
sequences completely.

For one [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}, there are no histories with total
charge [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline} and one history with total charge
[\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}. Therefore,

[\\\[ (A_1,B_1)=(0,1). \\\]]{.math .display}

For two [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} charges,

[\\\[ A_2=B_1=1, \\qquad B_2=A_1+B_1=1. \\\]]{.math .display}

For three,

[\\\[ A_3=B_2=1, \\qquad B_3=A_2+B_2=2. \\\]]{.math .display}

Continuing through seven anyons gives:

::: {.table-scroll aria-label="Scrollable data table" role="region" tabindex="0"}
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                 Number               total                 total    sum of sectors
        [\\(n\\)]{.math     [\\(1\\)]{.math   [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math 
            .inline} of           .inline}:             .inline}: 
    [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math   [\\(A_n\\)]{.math     [\\(B_n\\)]{.math 
        .inline} anyons            .inline}              .inline} 
  --------------------- ------------------- --------------------- -----------------
                      2                   1                     1                 2

                      3                   1                     2                 3

                      4                   2                     3                 5

                      5                   3                     5                 8

                      6                   5                     8                13

                      7                   8                    13                21
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
:::

The final column sums the dimensions of two distinct total-charge
sectors, recording a direct sum rather than a single coherent
computational space.

A superselection rule forbids ordinary coherent superpositions between
total charge [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline} and total charge
[\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} states. Computation therefore fixes the
total charge and works within one sector; the direct sum across sectors
is not generally usable as a qubit.

The two columns contain the sequences [\\(1,1,2,3,5,8,\\ldots\\)]{.math
.inline} and [\\(1,2,3,5,8,13,\\ldots\\)]{.math .inline}. In each
sequence, every entry is the sum of the preceding two entries.

These are the Fibonacci numbers. Define them by [\\(F_0=0\\)]{.math
.inline}, [\\(F_1=1\\)]{.math .inline}, and
[\\(F\_{n+1}=F_n+F\_{n-1}\\)]{.math .inline} for [\\(n\\ge1\\)]{.math
.inline}. Then

[\\\[ A_n=F\_{n-1},\\qquad B_n=F_n. \\\]]{.math .display}

Thus, the table follows solely from the fusion rule
[\[R135\]](#ref-R135 "[R135] S. Trebst, M. Troyer, Z. Wang, and A. W. W. Ludwig, “A
short introduction to Fibonacci anyon models,” Progress of Theoretical
Physics Supplement 176, 384–407 (2008). DOI: 10.1143/PTPS.176.384 ;
arXiv: 0902.3275 ."){.citation}. The theory is named after this
Fibonacci growth of its fusion spaces.
::::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Matrix recurrence, Fibonacci growth, and quantum dimension

The recurrence relation can be represented by a [\\(2\\times2\\)]{.math
.inline} matrix. In the ordered charge basis [\\((1,\\tau)\\)]{.math
.inline}, define the fusion matrix

[\\\[ N\_\\tau = \\begin{pmatrix} 0&1\\\\ 1&1 \\end{pmatrix}.
\\\]]{.math .display}

The matrix [\\(N\_\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} updates the pair of
fusion-path counts according to the recurrence above. Its powers
therefore generate Fibonacci numbers.

Let [\\(V_c\^{a_1\\cdots a_n}\\)]{.math .inline} denote the complex
vector space of fusion states in which the charges
[\\(a_1,\\ldots,a_n\\)]{.math .inline} have fixed total charge
[\\(c\\)]{.math .inline}. The dimensions of the two fixed-charge sectors
are

[\\\[ \\dim V_1\^{\\tau\^n}=F\_{n-1},\\qquad \\dim
V\_\\tau\^{\\tau\^n}=F_n. \\\]]{.math .display}

Here [\\(\\tau\^n\\)]{.math .inline} denotes [\\(n\\)]{.math .inline}
copies of [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}, not an ordinary numerical power.
Every fusion multiplicity in this theory is either zero or one.
Therefore, each valid labeling of a fusion tree corresponds to one basis
vector.

These dimensions grow exponentially at large [\\(n\\)]{.math .inline}.
The ratio of neighboring Fibonacci numbers approaches the largest
eigenvalue of [\\(N\_\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}. Its characteristic
equation is [\\(\\lambda\^2-\\lambda-1=0\\)]{.math .inline}, whose
positive root is

[\\\[ \\varphi=\\frac{1+\\sqrt5}{2}\\approx1.618. \\\]]{.math .display}

The number [\\(\\varphi\\)]{.math .inline} is the golden ratio. In this
context, it appears as the asymptotic growth rate of the fusion-space
dimension.

The quantum dimension [\\(d_a\\)]{.math .inline} of a charge
[\\(a\\)]{.math .inline} is the positive number compatible with the
fusion coefficients [\\(N\_{ab}\^{c}\\)]{.math .inline}, where
[\\(N\_{ab}\^{c}\\)]{.math .inline} is the multiplicity of charge
[\\(c\\)]{.math .inline} in the fusion of [\\(a\\)]{.math .inline} and
[\\(b\\)]{.math .inline}:

[\\\[ d_a d_b=\\sum_c N\_{ab}\^{c}d_c. \\\]]{.math .display}

Set [\\(d_1=1\\)]{.math .inline}. Applying this relation to
[\\(\\tau\\times\\tau=1+\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} gives

[\\\[ d\_\\tau\^2=1+d\_\\tau. \\\]]{.math .display}

Solving [\\(d\_\\tau\^2-d\_\\tau-1=0\\)]{.math .inline} yields
[\\((1\\pm\\sqrt5)/2\\)]{.math .inline}. A unitary fusion theory selects
the positive Perron--Frobenius solution, where the Perron--Frobenius
solution is the positive eigenvalue associated with a nonnegative fusion
matrix:

[\\\[ d\_\\tau=\\varphi=\\frac{1+\\sqrt5}{2}\\approx1.618. \\\]]{.math
.display}

Therefore, [\\(\\varphi\\)]{.math .inline} has three equivalent
interpretations: it is the largest eigenvalue of [\\(N\_\\tau\\)]{.math
.inline}, the limit of [\\(F\_{n+1}/F_n\\)]{.math .inline}, and the
quantum dimension of [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}. The number of fusion
states consequently scales as a constant times [\\(\\varphi\^n\\)]{.math
.inline}.

Quantum dimension is dimensionless and need not be an integer. It
characterizes the asymptotic growth of a nonlocal fusion space rather
than the number of local energy levels
[\[R135\]](#ref-R135 "[R135] S. Trebst, M. Troyer, Z. Wang, and A. W. W. Ludwig, “A
short introduction to Fibonacci anyon models,” Progress of Theoretical
Physics Supplement 176, 384–407 (2008). DOI: 10.1143/PTPS.176.384 ;
arXiv: 0902.3275 ."){.citation};
[\[R015\]](#ref-R015 "[R015] C. Nayak, S. H. Simon, A. Stern, M. Freedman, and S. Das
Sarma, “Non-Abelian Anyons and Topological Quantum Computation,” Reviews
of Modern Physics 80, 1083–1159 (2008). DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.80.1083 ;
arXiv: 0707.1889 ."){.citation}. In particular, a single
[\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} does not possess "1.618 states."
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Channel-dependent phases under exchange

Fusion histories label a degenerate state space nonlocally, through the
collective fusion outcomes, rather than through local degrees of freedom
attached independently to each particle. Exchanging neighboring
[\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} charges acts as a unitary transformation on
this fusion space.

An exchanged pair in a definite fusion channel contributes the phase
belonging to that channel. Exchanging a different pair calls for a
change of basis first: express the state with that pair fusing first,
apply the exchange phases, and transform back to the original basis. In
the notation of the previous chapter, this procedure is
[\\(F\^{-1}RF\\)]{.math .inline}.

A basis transformation followed by unequal channel-dependent phases
generally fails to commute with the same steps in a different order, so
exchanges of different neighboring pairs generate different rotations of
the encoded state.

Repeated exchanges build up a large set of rotations. For the Fibonacci
theory, this set approximates the gates required for quantum
computation; the density statement below makes the claim precise and
states its limitations.

An engineered Hamiltonian earns identification with the Fibonacci theory
by reproducing both the fusion spaces and the braiding data: the value
[\\(1.618\\)]{.math .inline} appearing in one observable is not enough
on its own. A claim of passive protection further requires these data to
arise as the low-energy physics of a gapped two-dimensional many-body
phase.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Three-anyon qubit encoding

Consider three [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} anyons with total charge
fixed to [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}. Since [\\(B_3=2\\)]{.math
.inline}, this sector is two-dimensional and can encode one logical
qubit:

[\\\[ \\begin{aligned}
\|0_L\\rangle&=\|((\\tau\\tau)\_1\\tau)\_\\tau\\rangle,\\\\
\|1_L\\rangle&=\|((\\tau\\tau)\_\\tau\\tau)\_\\tau\\rangle.
\\end{aligned} \\\]]{.math .display}

The subscript on a parenthesized group denotes that group's total
charge. The logical qubit is encoded in whether the first pair fuses to
[\\(1\\)]{.math .inline} or to [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}, while the
total charge of all three anyons remains fixed at [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math
.inline}.

Each individual particle keeps local topological charge
[\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}, so the logical information resides in the
pair outcome rather than on any single anyon.

Four [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} anyons with total charge
[\\(1\\)]{.math .inline} also provide a two-dimensional fusion space
because [\\(A_4=2\\)]{.math .inline}. This encoding is often preferred
because each encoded block has vacuum total charge. The three-anyon
encoding with total charge [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} is the smallest
example, so it is used for the following calculation.

Dropping the total-charge constraint leaves two states in different
superselection sectors, which do not constitute an ordinary qubit:
coherence between such sectors is generally unavailable as a
computational degree of freedom.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Braid matrices for the first and second pairs

The goal of this section is one concrete result: braiding the three
anyons --- a purely topological operation --- acts on the encoded qubit
as an ordinary [\\(2\\times2\\)]{.math .inline} unitary, and the two
neighboring braids do not commute. The recipe is the one built in
Chapter 14: exchanging the adjacent pair is the diagonal [\\(R\\)]{.math
.inline}-matrix, and exchanging the other pair is the same
[\\(R\\)]{.math .inline} conjugated by the recoupling [\\(F\\)]{.math
.inline}. Everything below is that recipe with the Fibonacci numbers
filled in.

Adopt the convention of Ref.
[\[R135\]](#ref-R135 "[R135] S. Trebst, M. Troyer, Z. Wang, and A. W. W. Ludwig, “A
short introduction to Fibonacci anyon models,” Progress of Theoretical
Physics Supplement 176, 384–407 (2008). DOI: 10.1143/PTPS.176.384 ;
arXiv: 0902.3275 ."){.citation}: fusion trees point downward, basis
channels are ordered as [\\((1,\\tau)\\)]{.math .inline}, and the
positive braid generator is the review's right-handed exchange with time
directed upward. Define

[\\\[ r_1=e\^{4\\pi i/5},\\qquad r\_\\tau=e\^{-3\\pi i/5}. \\\]]{.math
.display}

Exchanging anyons 1 and 2 is diagonal in the logical basis:

[\\\[ \\rho(\\sigma_1)=R = \\begin{pmatrix} r_1&0\\\\ 0&r\_\\tau
\\end{pmatrix}. \\\]]{.math .display}

Here [\\(\\sigma_i\\)]{.math .inline} denotes the positive exchange of
anyons [\\(i\\)]{.math .inline} and [\\(i+1\\)]{.math .inline}, and
[\\(\\rho\\)]{.math .inline} is the matrix representation of that
exchange on the fusion space. To exchange anyons 2 and 3, the basis must
first be changed so that those two anyons fuse first. The required
transformation is

[\\\[ F = \\begin{pmatrix} \\varphi\^{-1}&\\varphi\^{-1/2}\\\\
\\varphi\^{-1/2}&-\\varphi\^{-1} \\end{pmatrix}, \\qquad
\\varphi=\\frac{1+\\sqrt5}{2}. \\\]]{.math .display}

In this gauge, [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline} is real and symmetric, and
[\\(F\^{-1}=F\\)]{.math .inline}. Therefore,

[\\\[ \\rho(\\sigma_2)=FRF = \\begin{pmatrix}
\\varphi\^{-2}r_1+\\varphi\^{-1}r\_\\tau &
\\varphi\^{-3/2}(r_1-r\_\\tau)\\\\ \\varphi\^{-3/2}(r_1-r\_\\tau)&
\\varphi\^{-1}r_1+\\varphi\^{-2}r\_\\tau \\end{pmatrix}. \\\]]{.math
.display}

Applying this braid once to [\\(\|0_L\\rangle\\)]{.math .inline}
produces a state determined by the first column of
[\\(\\rho(\\sigma_2)\\)]{.math .inline}. Both entries are nonzero, so
the braid creates a coherent superposition of the two fusion channels.
If the first pair is then fused and its charge measured, this prepared
state gives

[\\\[ P(1)=\\varphi\^{-2},\\qquad P(\\tau)=\\varphi\^{-1}. \\\]]{.math
.display}

These probabilities sum to one because
[\\(\\varphi\^{-2}+\\varphi\^{-1}=1\\)]{.math .inline}. This identity
provides their normalization.

The values apply only to this initial state, this braid, and this
measurement. They are not universal probabilities for arbitrary
encounters between two [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} anyons.

Because [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline} is diagonal whereas [\\(FRF\\)]{.math
.inline} has nonzero off-diagonal entries,

[\\\[
\\rho(\\sigma_1)\\rho(\\sigma_2)\\neq\\rho(\\sigma_2)\\rho(\\sigma_1).
\\\]]{.math .display}

Thus, neighboring exchanges do not commute on this two-dimensional
fusion space. This is the smallest explicit demonstration of non-Abelian
statistics in the Fibonacci theory.

If the two channel phases were instead equal, so that
[\\(r_1=r\_\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}, then [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline} would
be proportional to the identity and would represent only a global phase.
The matrix [\\(FRF\\)]{.math .inline} would be the same global phase,
and the neighboring braid generators would commute.

The off-diagonal entries therefore require both ingredients: the
recoupling move mixes fusion channels, and unequal exchange phases
convert that mixing into a nontrivial transformation.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Consistency and gauge dependence of the [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}- and [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-symbols

For three [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} anyons with total charge
[\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}, the two fusion bases are

[\\\[ \|((\\tau\\tau)\_x\\tau)\_\\tau\\rangle, \\qquad
\|(\\tau(\\tau\\tau)\_y)\_\\tau\\rangle, \\\]]{.math .display}

where [\\(x,y\\in\\{1,\\tau\\}\\)]{.math .inline}. The matrix
[\\(F\^{\\tau\\tau\\tau}\_\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} transforms between
these two parenthesizations.

In the gauge adopted above, [\\(F\^{\\tau\\tau\\tau}\_\\tau\\)]{.math
.inline} is the matrix [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline} already used. All other
allowed [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-moves in this theory are scalars and
can be chosen to equal one.

The pentagon equation is the consistency condition requiring every
sequence of [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-moves between two parenthesizations
of four charges to give the same result. It expresses associativity of
fusion at the level of fusion-space basis transformations.

The scalar [\\(R_c\^{\\tau\\tau}\\)]{.math .inline} is the phase
associated with the chosen handed exchange of two [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math
.inline} charges whose combined charge is [\\(c\\)]{.math .inline}. In
the present convention,

[\\\[ R_1\^{\\tau\\tau}=e\^{4\\pi i/5},\\qquad
R\_\\tau\^{\\tau\\tau}=e\^{-3\\pi i/5}. \\\]]{.math .display}

The hexagon equations impose compatibility between recoupling
transformations and braiding. Together, the fusion rules, unitary
[\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-symbols, and [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-symbols
define the braid representation used here
[\[R135\]](#ref-R135 "[R135] S. Trebst, M. Troyer, Z. Wang, and A. W. W. Ludwig, “A
short introduction to Fibonacci anyon models,” Progress of Theoretical
Physics Supplement 176, 384–407 (2008). DOI: 10.1143/PTPS.176.384 ;
arXiv: 0902.3275 ."){.citation};
[\[R015\]](#ref-R015 "[R015] C. Nayak, S. H. Simon, A. Stern, M. Freedman, and S. Das
Sarma, “Non-Abelian Anyons and Topological Quantum Computation,” Reviews
of Modern Physics 80, 1083–1159 (2008). DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.80.1083 ;
arXiv: 0707.1889 ."){.citation}.

The individual matrix entries displayed above are not
convention-independent observables. Rephasing the one-dimensional fusion
and splitting vertices changes individual [\\(F\\)]{.math
.inline}-symbols and can also change the representatives of the
[\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-symbols, while leaving complete diagrams and
physical probabilities invariant. This freedom is a gauge freedom in the
sense introduced in the previous chapter. A matrix representation must
therefore be accompanied by its basis order, fusion-tree orientation,
gauge choice, and braid orientation.

Reversing braid handedness replaces [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline} by
[\\(R\^{-1}=R\^\\dagger\\)]{.math .inline}. Passing to the mirror theory
complex-conjugates the braiding data.

Different references may therefore display complex-conjugate phases
while describing equivalent physical content. Comparisons should use
gauge-invariant braid words, fusion probabilities, and link amplitudes
rather than isolated signs or matrix entries.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Density and braid universality

For [\\(n\\)]{.math .inline} anyons, the braid generators obey the two
relations introduced in Chapter 13:

[\\\[ \\sigma_i\\sigma\_{i+1}\\sigma_i
=\\sigma\_{i+1}\\sigma_i\\sigma\_{i+1}, \\qquad
\\sigma_i\\sigma_j=\\sigma_j\\sigma_i\\quad (\|i-j\|\\ge2). \\\]]{.math
.display}

The [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}- and [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-data map
these abstract generators to unitary matrices
[\\(\\rho(\\sigma_i)\\)]{.math .inline} acting on a fixed-total-charge
fusion space.

\[Theory\] For the Fibonacci theory's data, the resulting braid
representations are dense, up to a physically irrelevant overall phase,
in the unitary transformations on the computational fusion spaces. In
particular, the two three-anyon matrices above generate a dense set of
single-qubit rotations.

Suitable braids involving multiple anyons can approximate entangling
operations. This property is the mathematical basis of braid
universality
[\[R015\]](#ref-R015 "[R015] C. Nayak, S. H. Simon, A. Stern, M. Freedman, and S. Das
Sarma, “Non-Abelian Anyons and Topological Quantum Computation,” Reviews
of Modern Physics 80, 1083–1159 (2008). DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.80.1083 ;
arXiv: 0707.1889 ."){.citation};
[\[R136\]](#ref-R136 "[R136] M. H. Freedman, M. Larsen, and Z. Wang, “A modular functor
which is universal for quantum computation,” Communications in
Mathematical Physics 227, 605–622 (2002). DOI: 10.1007/s002200200645 ;
arXiv: quant-ph/0001108 ."){.citation}.

Numerical compilation algorithms explicitly construct braid words that
approximate specified target gates
[\[R137\]](#ref-R137 "[R137] L. Hormozi, G. Zikos, N. E. Bonesteel, and S. H. Simon,
“Topological quantum compiling,” Physical Review B 75, 165310 (2007).
DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevB.75.165310 ;
arXiv: quant-ph/0610111 ."){.citation}.

More precisely, density means that for any target unitary
[\\(U\\)]{.math .inline} and any tolerance [\\(\\varepsilon\>0\\)]{.math
.inline}, there is a finite braid word [\\(w\\)]{.math .inline} such
that

[\\\[ \\min\_\\alpha\\\|\\rho(w)-e\^{i\\alpha}U\\\|\<\\varepsilon,
\\\]]{.math .display}

where [\\(\\\|\\cdot\\\|\\)]{.math .inline} is an operator norm and
[\\(e\^{i\\alpha}\\)]{.math .inline} is a global phase. This definition
promises approximation by some finite braid word, leaving open both
single-exchange implementation and knowledge of the shortest word.

This density property is conventionally called universality. The term
must be interpreted specifically as the ability to approximate the
relevant unitary transformations. It leaves two further questions
separate: which braids serve as valid computational gates, and whether a
laboratory realization constitutes a complete quantum computer.

The fusion rule alone establishes Fibonacci growth and, in a unitary
theory, fixes [\\(d\_\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}; braid universality needs
more. The universality result depends on the particular consistent and
unitary [\\(F/R\\)]{.math .inline} data of the braided category.

A fusion ring specifying fusion algebra defines no braid representation
on its own.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Leakage outside the computational subspace

For encodings containing several logical qubits, the full fixed-charge
fusion space is generally larger than the selected tensor-product
computational subspace. A braid that does not preserve the chosen
subspace can populate these additional states.

This transition out of the computational subspace is called leakage.
Universality does not imply that every braid is leakage-free
[\[R015\]](#ref-R015 "[R015] C. Nayak, S. H. Simon, A. Stern, M. Freedman, and S. Das
Sarma, “Non-Abelian Anyons and Topological Quantum Computation,” Reviews
of Modern Physics 80, 1083–1159 (2008). DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.80.1083 ;
arXiv: 0707.1889 ."){.citation};
[\[R137\]](#ref-R137 "[R137] L. Hormozi, G. Zikos, N. E. Bonesteel, and S. H. Simon,
“Topological quantum compiling,” Physical Review B 75, 165310 (2007).
DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevB.75.165310 ;
arXiv: quant-ph/0610111 ."){.citation}. In the ideal theory, universal
compilation can suppress leakage to arbitrary accuracy. A complete
computer also requires initialization and fusion measurement.

If the additional fusion states are omitted from the analysis, a braid
can appear to act correctly on the intended logical states even though
it transfers amplitude outside the computational subspace. An error
estimate that ignores this leakage is therefore incomplete.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Relation to laboratory systems

The preceding equations define an ideal topological theory rather than a
specific material realization.

\[Theory\] The [\\(k=3\\)]{.math .inline} Read--Rezayi fractional
quantum Hall state was proposed to support a non-Abelian sector related
to these anyons
[\[R139\]](#ref-R139 "[R139] N. Read and E. Rezayi, “Beyond paired quantum Hall states:
Parafermions and incompressible states in the first excited Landau
level,” Physical Review B 59, 8084–8092 (1999). DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevB.59.8084 ;
arXiv: cond-mat/9809384 ."){.citation}. Observation of a Hall plateau at
a compatible filling would not, by itself, determine the complete fusion
and braiding data. In the literature surveyed through August 2026,
intrinsic Fibonacci exchange and fusion have not been established in a
defect crystal.

\[Experiment\] In 2024, Xu and collaborators used 27 superconducting
transmon qubits to prepare and manipulate a digital representation of a
Fibonacci Levin--Wen string-net state. They applied circuits
representing creation, fusion, and braiding and measured signatures
consistent with the target model
[\[R138\]](#ref-R138 "[R138] S. Xu et al., “Non-Abelian braiding of Fibonacci anyons with a
superconducting processor,” Nature Physics 20, 1469–1475 (2024)."){.citation}.

This result constitutes a substantial laboratory demonstration of
compiled string-net operations. Its microscopic excitations were
actively driven defects of the gate sequence rather than passively
emergent, mobile quasiparticles of a static transmon Hamiltonian.

The implemented string-net target was doubled Fibonacci order, and its
operations were compiled gates acting on ordinary physical qubits
[\[R138\]](#ref-R138 "[R138] S. Xu et al., “Non-Abelian braiding of Fibonacci anyons with a
superconducting processor,” Nature Physics 20, 1469–1475 (2024)."){.citation}.

\[Experiment\] A 2026 trapped-ion experiment prepared a 54-qubit state
of the [\\(S_3\\)]{.math .inline} quantum double and demonstrated a
universal gate set by combining braiding with fusion
[\[R140\]](#ref-R140 "[R140] C. F. B. Lo et al., “Universal gates from braiding and fusing
anyons on quantum hardware,” Nature 655, 591–597 (2026)."){.citation}.
This experiment provides a relevant control case because its anyons were
digitally encoded and its topological order was [\\(S_3\\)]{.math
.inline}, not Fibonacci. The phrase "universal anyon computation" does
not uniquely identify the underlying anyon theory.

A processor executing an [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline} gate simulates an
algebraic basis transformation. Establishing an equilibrium Fibonacci
phase or passive topological memory requires evidence of emergent
excitations in a gapped phase together with measured fusion and braiding
data.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Distinct meanings of Fibonacci implementations

- **Encoded Fibonacci qubit:** Information is stored in a fixed-charge
  fusion space of [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} anyons.

- **Emergent Fibonacci anyons:** These are quasiparticles of a gapped
  two-dimensional many-body phase whose adiabatic exchanges realize the
  Fibonacci braid representation.

- **Doubled Fibonacci:** This is the nonchiral Drinfeld-center theory
  produced by a Levin--Wen model using this chapter's input data. Its
  complete charge set and topological order are larger than those of the
  two-object chiral theory
  [\[R018\]](#ref-R018 "[R018] M. A. Levin and X.-G. Wen, “String-Net Condensation: A
  Physical Mechanism for Topological Phases,” Physical Review B 71, 045110
  (2005)."){.citation}.

- **Fibonacci-like digital simulation:** Ordinary hardware qubits encode
  fusion labels, while programmed gates implement [\\(F\\)]{.math
  .inline}, [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}, or string operators. Such a
  simulation can test the algebra without providing intrinsic
  quasiparticles or passive protection
  [\[R138\]](#ref-R138 "[R138] S. Xu et al., “Non-Abelian braiding of Fibonacci anyons with a
  superconducting processor,” Nature Physics 20, 1469–1475 (2024)."){.citation}.

Doubled Fibonacci is a genuine topological order distinct from the
chiral Fibonacci theory, containing computationally useful
Fibonacci-type sectors. A digital simulation is scientifically useful
for testing circuits and measurement protocols. The distinction among
these implementations is which physical system carries the topological
order and what mechanism, if any, supplies protection.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Common conceptual errors

- **Inferring universality from [\\(\\tau\\times\\tau=1+\\tau\\)]{.math
  .inline} alone.**

  The fusion rule determines state counting but does not determine braid
  phases. Pentagon- and hexagon-consistent unitary [\\(F/R\\)]{.math
  .inline} data are essential. Without the braid data, Fibonacci growth
  remains, but no density theorem follows.

- **Interpreting [\\(d\_\\tau=1.618\\ldots\\)]{.math .inline} as a local
  degeneracy.**

  A single anyon does not have "1.618 states." Quantum dimension
  describes the asymptotic growth of a nonlocal fusion space. The
  appearance of [\\(\\varphi\\)]{.math .inline} in a spectrum does not
  by itself demonstrate the required fusion spaces.

- **Combining distinct total-charge sectors as one encoding space.**

  The sum [\\(A_n+B_n\\)]{.math .inline} does not automatically define
  one coherent Hilbert space available for encoding. The boundary charge
  must be fixed before logical states are counted. Otherwise, the count
  refers to a direct sum of superselection sectors rather than a qubit.

- **Quoting matrices without their conventions.**

  Changes in basis phases, basis order, braid handedness, or mirror
  chirality alter the displayed matrices. Gauge-invariant braid words,
  fusion probabilities, and link amplitudes should be compared instead
  of isolated signs.

- **Equating braid universality with a fault-tolerant device.**

  \[Theory\] Ideal adiabatic braids are insensitive to small path
  deformations when the anyons remain separated in a gapped phase
  [\[R015\]](#ref-R015 "[R015] C. Nayak, S. H. Simon, A. Stern, M. Freedman, and S. Das
  Sarma, “Non-Abelian Anyons and Topological Quantum Computation,” Reviews
  of Modern Physics 80, 1083–1159 (2008). DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.80.1083 ;
  arXiv: 0707.1889 ."){.citation}.

  Real systems can nevertheless experience thermal anyon creation,
  quasiparticle poisoning, finite-separation splitting, diabatic
  transitions, control errors, and faulty readout. Universality
  specifies which gates can be approximated. Protection specifies how
  physical errors scale.

- **Ignoring leakage in multi-qubit encodings.**

  The physical fusion space can contain states outside the computational
  tensor product. A compilation procedure must control leakage as well
  as gate error
  [\[R137\]](#ref-R137 "[R137] L. Hormozi, G. Zikos, N. E. Bonesteel, and S. H. Simon,
  “Topological quantum compiling,” Physical Review B 75, 165310 (2007).
  DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevB.75.165310 ;
  arXiv: quant-ph/0610111 ."){.citation}.

- **Treating a circuit implementation as evidence of emergence.**

  A processor that executes an [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline} gate has
  simulated an algebraic transformation. It has not thereby acquired an
  equilibrium Fibonacci phase or passive topological memory.

- **Classifying every non-Abelian platform as Fibonacci.**

  Ising anyons, finite-group quantum doubles, and Fibonacci anyons have
  different fusion and braid data. "Non-Abelian" describes a broad class
  rather than a specific model.
:::

::: {.section .topic math-section=""}
### Exercises and answers

- **Derive the recurrence relations [\\(A\_{n+1}=B_n\\)]{.math .inline}
  and [\\(B\_{n+1}=A_n+B_n\\)]{.math .inline} from the fusion rule.**

  Only a previous total charge [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} can fuse
  with a new [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} to produce [\\(1\\)]{.math
  .inline}, so [\\(A\_{n+1}=B_n\\)]{.math .inline}. A new total charge
  [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline} can arise from either a previous
  [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline} or a previous [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline},
  so [\\(B\_{n+1}=A_n+B_n\\)]{.math .inline}.

- **Find the positive solution of [\\(d\_\\tau\^2=1+d\_\\tau\\)]{.math
  .inline}.**

  Solving the quadratic gives [\\((1\\pm\\sqrt5)/2\\)]{.math .inline}.
  Unitarity selects the positive root,

  [\\\[ \\varphi=\\frac{1+\\sqrt5}{2}. \\\]]{.math .display}

  The same quadratic is the characteristic equation of
  [\\(N\_\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}.

- **Identify where the logical information is stored in the three-anyon
  encoding.**

  It is stored in whether the first pair has fusion channel
  [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline} or [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math .inline}, while the
  total charge of all three anyons remains fixed at [\\(\\tau\\)]{.math
  .inline}.

- **Determine the consequence of equal channel phases in [\\(R\\)]{.math
  .inline}.**

  If the channel phases are equal, [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline} is a global
  phase on the two-dimensional space. Then [\\(FRF\\)]{.math .inline} is
  the same global phase, neighboring braids commute, and the non-Abelian
  action disappears.

- **State what cannot be concluded from the fusion rule alone.**

  The fusion rule establishes Fibonacci growth and, in a unitary theory,
  [\\(d\_\\tau=\\varphi\\)]{.math .inline}. It does not provide the
  braid phases or establish the density theorem. A fusion ring is not a
  braid representation.

- **Assess whether the 27-transmon experiment created intrinsic chiral
  Fibonacci matter.**

  The experiment digitally implemented a doubled-Fibonacci string-net
  state and associated operations on ordinary qubits. That
  implementation does not establish intrinsic chiral-Fibonacci matter
  [\[R138\]](#ref-R138 "[R138] S. Xu et al., “Non-Abelian braiding of Fibonacci anyons with a
  superconducting processor,” Nature Physics 20, 1469–1475 (2024)."){.citation}.

The next chapter turns to a simpler non-universal phase, the toric code,
and shows how local Hamiltonian terms produce anyons and nonlocal
logical sectors.
:::
