[← Appendix C --- Groups, spin rotations, and braid
representations](#appendix-c-groups-spin-rotations-and-braid-representations)[Appendix
E --- Consistency of alternative fusion trees
→](#appendix-e-consistency-of-alternative-fusion-trees)

## Appendix E --- Consistency of alternative fusion trees

A fusion tree for several anyons records the order in which pairs
combine and the intermediate charge at each step. Two trees with the
same incoming charges and the same total charge can span the same state
space in different bases. Consistency means the bookkeeping never leaks
into the physics: two sequences of basis changes that start and end at
the same trees compose to the same linear map.

Background, scope, and supporting argument

::: {.detail-body math-section=""}
Take three particles in a line carrying topological charges
[\\(a\\)]{.math .inline}, [\\(b\\)]{.math .inline}, and [\\(c\\)]{.math
.inline}: each charge names the superselection sector of its excitation,
the sector no local operation can change. Fix their combined charge at
[\\(d\\)]{.math .inline}.

Two parenthesizations are possible. Either [\\(a\\)]{.math .inline} and
[\\(b\\)]{.math .inline} combine first and the result combines with
[\\(c\\)]{.math .inline}, or [\\(b\\)]{.math .inline} and
[\\(c\\)]{.math .inline} combine first and [\\(a\\)]{.math .inline}
joins the result. Nothing moves; only the grouping on paper changes.

Each parenthesization, together with its allowed intermediate charges,
defines one basis of the fixed-total-charge fusion space. Braid
calculations may run in either basis, and the translation between them
must leave every physical amplitude unchanged.
:::

::: chapter-tools
Show detailed notes
:::

:::: {.section .topic aria-labelledby="e.1-left-associated-and-right-associated-fusion-bases" math-section=""}
### E.1 Left-Associated and Right-Associated Fusion Bases

The two groupings, drawn with time running downward:

    ((a b)_e c)_d              (a (b c)_f)_d

    a   b   c                  a   b   c
     \ /    |                  |    \ /
      e     |                  |     f
       \   /                    \   /
        \ /                      \ /
         d                        d

Detailed treatment: left-associated and right-associated fusion bases

::: {.detail-body math-section=""}
#### Left-associated and right-associated fusion bases

Both diagrams read top to bottom: incoming charges at the top, total
charge at the bottom.

    Read top to bottom

    ((a b)_e c)_d              (a (b c)_f)_d

    a   b   c                  a   b   c
     \ /    |                  |    \ /
      e     |                  |     f
       \   /                    \   /
        \ /                      \ /
         d                        d

The internal labels [\\(e\\)]{.math .inline} and [\\(f\\)]{.math
.inline} are the intermediate charges allowed by the fusion rules. When
the same three labels can combine in several independent ways, each
vertex carries an extra basis label distinguishing the channels. Those
vertex bases are orthonormal.

A fusion tree is therefore a parenthesization plus a choice of
intermediate charges for fixed incoming and total labels. It names one
basis vector, not a collision history: nothing in the tree says one pair
of particles physically met before another.
:::
::::

:::: {.section .topic aria-labelledby="e.2-the-f-move" math-section=""}
### E.2 The F-Move

Above, [\\(a,b,c\\)]{.math .inline} enter and [\\(d\\)]{.math .inline}
exits. The left tree groups [\\(a\\)]{.math .inline} with
[\\(b\\)]{.math .inline} through [\\(e\\)]{.math .inline}; the right
tree groups [\\(b\\)]{.math .inline} with [\\(c\\)]{.math .inline}
through [\\(f\\)]{.math .inline}. The [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-move is
the change of basis between them:

[\\\[ \|((ab)\_e c)\_d; \\mu, \\nu\\rangle = \\sum\_{f,\\alpha,\\beta}
\[F\^{abc}\_d\]\_{(e,\\mu,\\nu)(f,\\alpha,\\beta)} \|(a(bc)\_f)\_d;
\\alpha, \\beta\\rangle \\\]]{.math .display}

The extra indices [\\(\\mu,\\nu\\)]{.math .inline} and
[\\(\\alpha,\\beta\\)]{.math .inline} select among parallel channels
when one triple of labels fuses in several independent ways. When every
triple fuses in at most one way --- a multiplicity-free theory --- those
indices drop out. The sum visits only channels the fusion rules allow.

An [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-move re-labels the same state; the particles
stay put. Appendix A changed coordinates on a vector; here the
coordinates are the intermediate charge labels.

Detailed treatment: associativity as a change of basis

::: {.detail-body math-section=""}
#### Associativity as a change of basis

Re-pairing the labels moves no particle. It re-expresses the same fusion
state in the other basis:

    a   b   c                  a   b   c
     \ /    |                  |    \ /
      e     |      -->         |     f
       \   /                    \   /
        \ /                      \ /
         d                        d

Let [\\(\\mu\\)]{.math .inline} label the vertex [\\(a,b\\to e\\)]{.math
.inline}, and let [\\(\\nu\\)]{.math .inline} label the vertex
[\\(e,c\\to d\\)]{.math .inline} in the left-associated tree. Let
[\\(\\alpha\\)]{.math .inline} label the vertex [\\(b,c\\to f\\)]{.math
.inline}, and let [\\(\\beta\\)]{.math .inline} label the vertex
[\\(a,f\\to d\\)]{.math .inline} in the right-associated tree. The
transformation between these bases is

[\\\[ \\big\|((ab)\_e c)\_d;\\mu,\\nu\\big\\rangle =
\\sum\_{f,\\alpha,\\beta}
\[F\^{abc}\_d\]\_{(e,\\mu,\\nu)(f,\\alpha,\\beta)}
\\big\|(a(bc)\_f)\_d;\\alpha,\\beta\\big\\rangle. \\\]]{.math .display}

Each vertex label enumerates the independent channels of its triple:
[\\(\\mu=1,\\ldots,N\_{ab}\^{e}\\)]{.math .inline},
[\\(\\nu=1,\\ldots,N\_{ec}\^{d}\\)]{.math .inline},
[\\(\\alpha=1,\\ldots,N\_{bc}\^{f}\\)]{.math .inline}, and
[\\(\\beta=1,\\ldots,N\_{af}\^{d}\\)]{.math .inline}. The integer
[\\(N\_{ab}\^{e}\\)]{.math .inline} counts how many independent ways
charges [\\(a\\)]{.math .inline} and [\\(b\\)]{.math .inline} reach
total charge [\\(e\\)]{.math .inline}.

Those matrix elements are the [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-symbols: the
entries of the basis-change matrix for this three-body space, recording
no additional physical event.

In a unitary anyon theory --- one whose fusion spaces carry inner
products preserved by all allowed maps --- [\\(F\^{abc}\_d\\)]{.math
.inline} is a unitary matrix on the fixed-[\\(d\\)]{.math .inline}
fusion space. Without unitarity the two trees still span the same
abstract space, but changing basis can distort norms, so probabilities
computed with a naive conjugate transpose come out wrong.
:::
::::

:::::: {.section .topic aria-labelledby="e.3-the-r-move" math-section=""}
### E.3 The R-Move

Once two anyons sit in a definite total channel [\\(c\\)]{.math
.inline}, exchanging their positions maps the fusion space for one
ordering to the space for the other:

[\\\[ R\^{ab}\_c : V\_{ab}\^c \\to V\_{ba}\^c \\\]]{.math .display}

Here [\\(V\_{ab}\^c\\)]{.math .inline} collects the distinct ways
[\\(a,b\\)]{.math .inline} fuse to [\\(c\\)]{.math .inline}. In a larger
tree the pair to be exchanged may sit apart; the standard maneuver
re-pairs the tree until the pair is adjacent, applies [\\(R\\)]{.math
.inline}, and returns with the inverse [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}.
Braiding matrices therefore mix recoupling entries with exchange phases.

Detailed treatment: oriented exchange of two charges

::: {.detail-body math-section=""}
#### Oriented exchange of two charges

Physically swapping two charges moves them. Fixing the total charge
[\\(c\\)]{.math .inline} and choosing the counterclockwise sense of the
swap gives the linear map

[\\\[ R\^{ab}\_c:V\_{ab}\^{c}\\longrightarrow V\_{ba}\^{c}. \\\]]{.math
.display}

Here [\\(V\_{ab}\^{c}\\)]{.math .inline} holds the distinct channels
through which [\\(a\\)]{.math .inline} and [\\(b\\)]{.math .inline}
reach total charge [\\(c\\)]{.math .inline}.

The entries of that map are the [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-symbols. An
[\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-move re-pairs labels on paper; an
[\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-move records a physical swap with a chosen
orientation.

In a multiplicity-free theory --- every triple fuses in at most one way
--- each allowed channel [\\(c\\)]{.math .inline} gives a single phase
[\\(R\^{ab}\_c\\)]{.math .inline}. With multiplicities present, the same
symbol denotes a unitary matrix mixing the parallel vertex channels.

The conventions fix domains with orientation: the clockwise swap of the
same pair is [\\((R\^{ba}\_c)\^{-1}\\)]{.math .inline}, with the labels
transposed and the map inverted. Complex-conjugating every
[\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-symbol reproduces that inverse only after the
charge labels and orientation conventions are matched; applied blindly
it gives the wrong operator.

Dropping the orientation labels collapses clockwise and counterclockwise
swaps onto the same notation while the operators differ. The hexagon
equations below compare specific oriented swaps, so they need those
labels kept.
:::

::: {.section .topic-extension math-section=""}
#### Three Ising [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline} anyons {#three-ising-anyons}

The Ising charges [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline}, [\\(\\psi\\)]{.math
.inline}, and [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline} satisfy the fusion rules

[\\\[ \\sigma\\times\\sigma=1+\\psi, \\qquad
\\psi\\times\\sigma=\\sigma, \\qquad \\psi\\times\\psi=1. \\\]]{.math
.display}

Take three [\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline} anyons with total charge
[\\(\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline}. In the left-associated tree the first
pair fuses through [\\(e\\in\\{1,\\psi\\}\\)]{.math .inline}. In the
standard gauge --- the standard choice of vertex basis phases ---

[\\\[ F\\equiv F\^{\\sigma\\sigma\\sigma}\_{\\sigma} =\\frac1{\\sqrt2}
\\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\\\1&-1\\end{pmatrix}, \\\]]{.math .display}

[\\\[ R\^{\\sigma\\sigma}\_{1}=e\^{-i\\pi/8}, \\qquad
R\^{\\sigma\\sigma}\_{\\psi}=e\^{3i\\pi/8}. \\\]]{.math .display}

Rows and columns of [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline} run in the order
[\\((1,\\psi)\\)]{.math .inline}. Multiplying the matrix by itself
returns the identity, which together with unitarity [\\(F\^\\dagger
F=I\\)]{.math .inline} gives [\\(F\^{-1}=F\\)]{.math .inline}. A state
carrying left intermediate channel [\\(e=1\\)]{.math .inline} therefore
reads in the right-associated basis as

[\\\[ \|1\\rangle_L=\\frac{\|1\\rangle_R+\|\\psi\\rangle_R}{\\sqrt2}.
\\\]]{.math .display}

Measuring the right intermediate channel then returns either outcome
with probability [\\(1/2\\)]{.math .inline}. The fusion rule lists the
two possible outcomes; the [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-matrix fixes the
amplitude of each.

Exchanging the first pair in the left-associated basis gives [\\\[
B_1=\\begin{pmatrix}R\^{\\sigma\\sigma}\_1&0\\\\0&R\^{\\sigma\\sigma}\_\\psi\\end{pmatrix}
=e\^{-i\\pi/8}\\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\\\0&i\\end{pmatrix} \\\]]{.math
.display}; the second pair is not adjacent there, so an [\\(F\\)]{.math
.inline}-move first re-pairs the tree to expose its channel:

[\\\[ B_2=FB_1F\^{-1} =\\frac{e\^{-i\\pi/8}}2
\\begin{pmatrix}1+i&1-i\\\\1-i&1+i\\end{pmatrix}. \\\]]{.math .display}

Writing [\\(D_0=\\operatorname{diag}(1,i)\\)]{.math .inline} for the
phase pattern and setting the common phase aside for a line, direct
multiplication gives

[\\\[ D_0(FD_0F)D_0=(FD_0F)D_0(FD_0F) =\\frac{1+i}{2}
\\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\\\1&-1\\end{pmatrix}. \\\]]{.math .display}

Multiplying the common phase [\\(e\^{-3i\\pi/8}\\)]{.math .inline} back
onto both sides gives

[\\\[ B_1B_2B_1=B_2B_1B_2. \\\]]{.math .display}

The local [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}- and [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-symbols
therefore assemble into matrices satisfying the three-strand braid
relation, while [\\(B_1B_2\\ne B_2B_1\\)]{.math .inline} keeps the
representation non-Abelian. Satisfying the braid relation leaves
commutativity open
[\[R015\]](#ref-R015 "[R015] C. Nayak, S. H. Simon, A. Stern, M. Freedman, and S. Das
Sarma, “Non-Abelian Anyons and Topological Quantum Computation,” Reviews
of Modern Physics 80, 1083–1159 (2008). DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.80.1083 ;
arXiv: 0707.1889 ."){.citation};
[\[R017\]](#ref-R017 "[R017] A. Kitaev, “Anyons in an Exactly Solved Model and Beyond,”
Annals of Physics 321, 2–111 (2006). DOI: 10.1016/j.aop.2005.10.005 ;
arXiv: cond-mat/0506438 ."){.citation}.
:::

::: {.section .topic-extension math-section=""}
#### The basis-independent associator

Before choosing bases at the fusion vertices, reassociation is the
abstract map

[\\\[ \\alpha\_{a,b,c}:(a\\otimes b)\\otimes c \\to a\\otimes(b\\otimes
c). \\\]]{.math .display}

At the categorical level the tensor product [\\(\\otimes\\)]{.math
.inline} combines charges, and [\\(\\alpha\\)]{.math .inline} is the
associator regrouping a triple. Choosing bases in the relevant fusion
spaces turns [\\(\\alpha\\)]{.math .inline} into a matrix whose entries
are the [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-symbols.

For fixed [\\(a,b,c,d\\)]{.math .inline}, orthonormal vertex bases turn
unitarity of the map into the matrix identity

[\\\[ \\sum\_{f,\\alpha,\\beta}
\[F\^{abc}\_d\]\_{(e,\\mu,\\nu)(f,\\alpha,\\beta)}
\[F\^{abc}\_d\]\^\*\_{(e\',\\mu\',\\nu\')(f,\\alpha,\\beta)} =
\\delta\_{ee\'}\\delta\_{\\mu\\mu\'}\\delta\_{\\nu\\nu\'}, \\\]]{.math
.display}

where [\\(\*\\)]{.math .inline} is complex conjugation and
[\\(\\delta\\)]{.math .inline} is one on equal indices and zero
otherwise. The identity needs orthonormal vertex bases: with
non-orthonormal bases the abstract associator [\\(\\alpha\\)]{.math
.inline} stays an isomorphism, but its matrix need not satisfy this
conjugate-transpose relation.
:::
::::::

::::::::::::::: {.section .topic aria-labelledby="e.4-the-pentagons-and-hexagons" math-section=""}
### E.4 The Pentagons and Hexagons

Four objects admit five parenthesizations, arranged as the five corners
the pentagon visits. The pentagon relation demands that the two routes
between the extreme corners compose to the same map. Writing the
associator as [\\(\\alpha\_{a,b,c}:(a\\otimes b)\\otimes c\\to
a\\otimes(b\\otimes c)\\)]{.math .inline}; each composite applies its
rightmost map first.

The pentagon equation:

[\\\[ \\alpha\_{a,b,c\\otimes d} \\circ \\alpha\_{a\\otimes b,c,d} =
(\\operatorname{id}\_a \\otimes \\alpha\_{b,c,d}) \\circ
\\alpha\_{a,b\\otimes c,d} \\circ (\\alpha\_{a,b,c} \\otimes
\\operatorname{id}\_d) \\\]]{.math .display}

Reassociation and braiding meet in the hexagon equations. Writing
[\\(\\beta\_{a,b}:a\\otimes b\\to b\\otimes a\\)]{.math .inline} for the
braiding map, the first hexagon moves one object past a fused pair in
one step and past its two constituents in two steps, with associators
bridging the two parenthesizations:

[\\\[ \\alpha\_{b,c,a} \\circ \\beta\_{a,b\\otimes c} \\circ
\\alpha\_{a,b,c} = (\\operatorname{id}\_b \\otimes \\beta\_{a,c}) \\circ
\\alpha\_{b,a,c} \\circ (\\beta\_{a,b} \\otimes \\operatorname{id}\_c)
\\\]]{.math .display}

[\\\[ \\alpha\^{-1}\_{c,a,b} \\circ \\beta\_{a\\otimes b,c} \\circ
\\alpha\^{-1}\_{a,b,c} = (\\beta\_{a,c} \\otimes \\operatorname{id}\_b)
\\circ \\alpha\^{-1}\_{a,c,b} \\circ (\\operatorname{id}\_a \\otimes
\\beta\_{b,c}) \\\]]{.math .display}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Detailed treatment: four-charge reassociation and the pentagon equation

::: {.detail-body math-section=""}
#### Four-charge reassociation and the pentagon equation

Reassociating four objects from [\\((((a\\otimes b)\\otimes c)\\otimes
d)\\)]{.math .inline} to [\\(a\\otimes(b\\otimes(c\\otimes d))\\)]{.math
.inline} offers two routes through the intermediate parenthesizations:

                      ((a b) (c d))
                     /             \
       (((a b) c) d)               (a (b (c d)))
            |                            |
       ((a (b c)) d)  ------------>  (a ((b c) d))

The upper route composes two associators; the lower route composes
three. The pentagon equation equates the two composites:

[\\\[ \\boxed{ \\alpha\_{a,b,c\\otimes d}\\circ\\alpha\_{a\\otimes
b,c,d} = (\\operatorname{id}\_a\\otimes\\alpha\_{b,c,d})
\\circ\\alpha\_{a,b\\otimes c,d}
\\circ(\\alpha\_{a,b,c}\\otimes\\operatorname{id}\_d) }. \\\]]{.math
.display}

Both composites run from the same source tree to the same target tree,
each read rightmost-first. Expanding the identity in fusion-tree bases
turns it into polynomial equations for the entries of the
[\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-matrices, summing over every allowed
intermediate charge and multiplicity label
[\[R022\]](#ref-R022 "[R022] G. Moore and N. Seiberg, “Classical and Quantum Conformal
Field Theory,” Communications in Mathematical Physics 123, 177–254
(1989). DOI: 10.1007/BF01238857 ."){.citation};
[\[R019\]](#ref-R019 "[R019] B. Bakalov and A. Kirillov Jr., Lectures on Tensor
Categories and Modular Functors, University Lecture Series 21, American
Mathematical Society (2001). DOI: 10.1090/ulect/021 ."){.citation}.

The equation is visible even in the simplest case: in a pointed model
with a gauge where every allowed fusion space is one-dimensional and
every associator is [\\(F=1\\)]{.math .inline}, the pentagon reads
[\\(1\\cdot1=1\\cdot1\\cdot1\\)]{.math .inline}.

Beyond that trivial case, pointed categories can carry phase-valued
associators classified by a group [\\(3\\)]{.math .inline}-cocycle, and
the pentagon equation becomes the cocycle condition. The Ising and
Fibonacci theories put nontrivial matrix-valued [\\(F\\)]{.math
.inline}-symbols through the same test.

The pentagon is a coherence condition in the strict sense: dropping it
lets a four-anyon amplitude depend on which sequence of intermediate
basis changes produced it, so no single linear map answers all routes.
:::

::: {.section .topic-extension math-section=""}
#### Braiding an object past a composite

The categorical braiding is the map

[\\\[ \\beta\_{a,b}:a\\otimes b\\to b\\otimes a \\\]]{.math .display}
Its matrix entries in chosen bases are the [\\(R\\)]{.math
.inline}-symbols. Moving [\\(a\\)]{.math .inline} past the composite
[\\(b\\otimes c\\)]{.math .inline} in one exchange must match moving
[\\(a\\)]{.math .inline} past [\\(b\\)]{.math .inline} and then past
[\\(c\\)]{.math .inline} in two. Each move starts and ends in a
different parenthesization, so associators bridge the exchanges on each
side.

Reading composites rightmost-first, the positive-crossing identity reads

[\\\[ \\boxed{ \\alpha\_{b,c,a}\\circ\\beta\_{a,b\\otimes
c}\\circ\\alpha\_{a,b,c} = (\\operatorname{id}\_b\\otimes\\beta\_{a,c})
\\circ\\alpha\_{b,a,c}
\\circ(\\beta\_{a,b}\\otimes\\operatorname{id}\_c) }. \\\]]{.math
.display}

Both composites run from [\\((a\\otimes b)\\otimes c\\)]{.math .inline}
to [\\(b\\otimes(c\\otimes a)\\)]{.math .inline}. The companion identity
moves a composite past [\\(c\\)]{.math .inline} instead:

[\\\[ \\boxed{ \\alpha\^{-1}\_{c,a,b}\\circ\\beta\_{a\\otimes
b,c}\\circ\\alpha\^{-1}\_{a,b,c} =
(\\beta\_{a,c}\\otimes\\operatorname{id}\_b)
\\circ\\alpha\^{-1}\_{a,c,b}
\\circ(\\operatorname{id}\_a\\otimes\\beta\_{b,c}) }. \\\]]{.math
.display}

Both composites run from [\\(a\\otimes(b\\otimes c)\\)]{.math .inline}
to [\\((c\\otimes a)\\otimes b\\)]{.math .inline}. Each identity strings
three exchanges and three regroupings into a six-sided loop; the hexagon
equations demand that loop compose to one unambiguous map.

With the pentagon equation, the hexagon equations guarantee that any two
labeled ribbon diagrams differing by allowed moves evaluate to the same
operator --- [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-moves and crossings assign each
equivalence class one value
[\[R022\]](#ref-R022 "[R022] G. Moore and N. Seiberg, “Classical and Quantum Conformal
Field Theory,” Communications in Mathematical Physics 123, 177–254
(1989). DOI: 10.1007/BF01238857 ."){.citation};
[\[R023\]](#ref-R023 "[R023] P. Bonderson, K. Shtengel, and J. K. Slingerland,
“Interferometry of Non-Abelian Anyons,” Annals of Physics 323, 2709–2755
(2008). DOI: 10.1016/j.aop.2008.01.012 ;
arXiv: 0707.4206 ."){.citation}. Each hexagon governs one side of the
tensor product: omitting the first leaves exchange past a right-hand
composite unconstrained, and omitting the second leaves exchange past a
left-hand composite unconstrained.

Written out in components, the first hexagon in a multiplicity-free
theory contributes, among others, the relation

[\\\[ R\^{ab}\_{e}\[F\^{bac}\_{d}\]\_{eg}R\^{ac}\_{g} = \\sum_f
\[F\^{abc}\_{d}\]\_{ef}R\^{a f}\_{d}\[F\^{bca}\_{d}\]\_{fg}. \\\]]{.math
.display}

The relation follows the downward-tree, counterclockwise-exchange
conventions of this appendix, with each basis change taken in the fixed
direction, and the sum visits only allowed intermediate charges
[\\(f\\)]{.math .inline}. Sources using upward-oriented trees, clockwise
[\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-symbols, or the inverse [\\(F\\)]{.math
.inline} convention print equations that look different and match after
the conventions are translated.
:::

::: {.section .topic-extension math-section=""}
#### Derivation of the braid relations

For three anyons in the left-associated basis, [\\(B_1\\)]{.math
.inline} applies [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline} to the first pair directly,
while [\\(B_2\\)]{.math .inline} reaches the second pair by the re-pair,
exchange, return maneuver: an [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-move, then an
[\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-move on the exposed pair, then the inverse
[\\(F\\)]{.math .inline}-move. Because the hexagon equations reconcile
exchange with fusion and the pentagon equation reconciles the
reassociation routes with each other, the two matrices satisfy

[\\\[ B_iB\_{i+1}B_i=B\_{i+1}B_iB\_{i+1}, \\qquad
B_iB_j=B_jB_i\\quad(\|i-j\|\\ge2). \\\]]{.math .display}

The Ising calculation above checks the three-strand identity on
two-by-two matrices. Those relations qualify matrices as a braid
representation; density of the image and computational universality are
further properties the relations alone leave undecided.
:::

::: {.section .topic-extension math-section=""}
#### Double braiding and monodromy

One exchange sends the ordered pair [\\(a,b\\)]{.math .inline} to the
opposite order. Winding one charge fully around the other and back ---
the double braid, or monodromy --- restores the order. In a
multiplicity-free fusion channel [\\(c\\)]{.math .inline} that closed
winding acts as

[\\\[ M\^{ab}\_{c}=R\^{ab}\_{c}R\^{ba}\_{c}. \\\]]{.math .display}

The single exchange moves between the two orderings; the double braid
starts and ends in the same ordering, which is why interferometry
measures the double braid.

In a ribbon theory --- braiding and twisting made mutually compatible
--- the double braid reduces to twist phases through the balancing
relation:

[\\\[ M\^{ab}\_{c}=\\frac{\\theta_c}{\\theta_a\\theta_b}, \\\]]{.math
.display}

where [\\(\\theta_x\\)]{.math .inline} is the phase of a
[\\(2\\pi\\)]{.math .inline} twist of the ribbon carrying simple charge
[\\(x\\)]{.math .inline}. Vertex rephasings of the kind described below
cancel out of this ratio, so the monodromy --- unlike either individual
[\\(R\\)]{.math .inline} phase on its own --- matches what an
interference experiment extracts
[\[R015\]](#ref-R015 "[R015] C. Nayak, S. H. Simon, A. Stern, M. Freedman, and S. Das
Sarma, “Non-Abelian Anyons and Topological Quantum Computation,” Reviews
of Modern Physics 80, 1083–1159 (2008). DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.80.1083 ;
arXiv: 0707.1889 ."){.citation};
[\[R023\]](#ref-R023 "[R023] P. Bonderson, K. Shtengel, and J. K. Slingerland,
“Interferometry of Non-Abelian Anyons,” Annals of Physics 323, 2709–2755
(2008). DOI: 10.1016/j.aop.2008.01.012 ;
arXiv: 0707.4206 ."){.citation}.

In the standard gauge the Ising twists read [\\(\\theta_1=1\\)]{.math
.inline}, [\\(\\theta\_\\psi=-1\\)]{.math .inline}, and
[\\(\\theta\_\\sigma=e\^{i\\pi/8}\\)]{.math .inline} for
[\\(a=b=\\sigma\\)]{.math .inline}. The vacuum channel then gives

[\\\[ M\^{\\sigma\\sigma}\_{1} =(e\^{-i\\pi/8})\^2=e\^{-i\\pi/4}
=\\frac{\\theta_1}{\\theta\_\\sigma\^2}, \\\]]{.math .display}

and the [\\(\\psi\\)]{.math .inline} channel gives

[\\\[ M\^{\\sigma\\sigma}\_{\\psi} =(e\^{3i\\pi/8})\^2=e\^{3i\\pi/4}
=\\frac{\\theta\_\\psi}{\\theta\_\\sigma\^2}. \\\]]{.math .display}

The two channels differ by that relative sign. Twist phases are quoted
up to an overall framing choice, so any table reporting them must name
the framing convention it uses.
:::

::: {.section .topic-extension math-section=""}
#### Gauge transformations of fusion vertices

Each fusion vertex admits its own choice of orthonormal basis. In a
multiplicity-free theory that freedom is one phase per vertex:

[\\\[ \|a,b;c\\rangle\' = u\^{ab}\_{c}\|a,b;c\\rangle, \\qquad
\|u\^{ab}\_{c}\|=1. \\\]]{.math .display}

Rephasing the vertices sends the symbols to

[\\\[ \[F\^{abc}\_d\]\'\_{ef} = \\frac{u\^{ab}\_{e}u\^{ec}\_{d}}
{u\^{bc}\_{f}u\^{af}\_{d}} \[F\^{abc}\_d\]\_{ef}, \\\]]{.math .display}

[\\\[ \[R\^{ab}\_{c}\]\' =
\\frac{u\^{ab}\_{c}}{u\^{ba}\_{c}}R\^{ab}\_{c}. \\\]]{.math .display}

With fusion multiplicities each [\\(u\\)]{.math .inline} widens to a
unitary matrix contracting the parallel channels. Either way the
transformation is a gauge change: the same physics written in a
different vertex basis.

The pentagon and hexagon equations hold in every gauge. Changing the
external computational basis conjugates the complete braid operators
accordingly.

A single entry such as [\\(\[F\]\_{ef}\\)]{.math .inline} shifts under
rephasing and carries no invariant meaning on its own. What survives
rephasing is the gauge-invariant content: fusion probabilities stated
with their vertex conventions, spectra and traces of closed braids,
topological spins, and modular data. Matching those quantities across
sources still needs the framing and overall-phase conventions spelled
out
[\[R015\]](#ref-R015 "[R015] C. Nayak, S. H. Simon, A. Stern, M. Freedman, and S. Das
Sarma, “Non-Abelian Anyons and Topological Quantum Computation,” Reviews
of Modern Physics 80, 1083–1159 (2008). DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.80.1083 ;
arXiv: 0707.1889 ."){.citation};
[\[R019\]](#ref-R019 "[R019] B. Bakalov and A. Kirillov Jr., Lectures on Tensor
Categories and Modular Functors, University Lecture Series 21, American
Mathematical Society (2001). DOI: 10.1090/ulect/021 ."){.citation}.

Mirroring reverses every crossing. In a unitary convention the mirrored
braiding data read as inverses or complex conjugates, but the
bookkeeping does not end there: orientation labels and framing phases
still need tracking. Chiral Fibonacci theory, its mirror, and the
doubled theory holding both therefore stay three distinct theories;
dropping a minus sign does not convert one into another.
:::

::: {.section .topic-extension math-section=""}
#### Limits of consistency tables

\[Theory\] A table of [\\(N\\)]{.math .inline}, [\\(F\\)]{.math
.inline}, and [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline} satisfying unitarity and the
pentagon and hexagon equations is internally consistent as topological
data. Internal consistency leaves two further questions open: whether a
local Hamiltonian realizes those data, and whether the corresponding
many-body system has a gap
[\[R017\]](#ref-R017 "[R017] A. Kitaev, “Anyons in an Exactly Solved Model and Beyond,”
Annals of Physics 321, 2–111 (2006). DOI: 10.1016/j.aop.2005.10.005 ;
arXiv: cond-mat/0506438 ."){.citation};
[\[R019\]](#ref-R019 "[R019] B. Bakalov and A. Kirillov Jr., Lectures on Tensor
Categories and Modular Functors, University Lecture Series 21, American
Mathematical Society (2001). DOI: 10.1090/ulect/021 ."){.citation}.

\[Numerics\] Approximate matrices extracted from a finite system come
with four mandatory appendices: the basis conventions, the finite-size
scaling, the measured leakage outside the proposed fusion space, and the
residual path dependence. Checking one braid word exercises one path;
the coherence structure comprises all of them.

\[Experiment\] A processor programmed with the Ising matrices above
demonstrates control over that representation to its measured accuracy
--- evidence about the gates, not about the medium. Intrinsic anyons
need evidence of a different kind: localized excitations, addressable
fusion sectors, and braid responses emerging from the device\'s
many-body physics. Writing anyonic labels on the basis vectors of an
encoded subspace supplies none of that evidence on its own.
:::

Common sources of error

:::: {.detail-body math-section=""}
::: {.section .topic-extension math-section=""}
#### Common sources of error

- Multiplying braid words using one temporal ordering convention while
  drawing them using the opposite convention.

- Applying [\\(F\\)]{.math .inline} where [\\(F\^{-1}\\)]{.math .inline}
  is required to return to the original fusion tree.

- Summing over forbidden intermediate labels instead of enforcing the
  fusion coefficients.

- Dropping the vertex labels that distinguish parallel channels when
  [\\(N\_{ab}\^{c}\>1\\)]{.math .inline}.

- Treating gauge-dependent symbol entries from different vertex-phase
  choices as physical disagreements.

- Calling residual pentagon and hexagon violations harmless numerical
  noise without checking them against the claimed precision.

- Concluding computational universality from noncommuting braid matrices
  alone --- density of the image is the further property universality
  needs.
:::
::::

Verification exercises

:::: {.detail-body math-section=""}
::: {.section .topic-extension math-section=""}
#### Verification exercises

Check that [\\(F\^{\\sigma\\sigma\\sigma}\_{\\sigma}\\)]{.math .inline}
squares to the identity.

Multiplying the displayed matrix by itself returns [\\(I\\)]{.math
.inline}, and with unitarity [\\(F\^\\dagger F=I\\)]{.math .inline} that
product is exactly [\\(F\^{-1}=F\\)]{.math .inline}.

What does one [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-symbol record?

An [\\(R\\)]{.math .inline}-symbol records one oriented exchange of two
charges fusing to the specified total channel.

Do both sides of the pentagon equation start and end at the same trees?

Each composite starts at [\\((((a\\otimes b)\\otimes c)\\otimes
d)\\)]{.math .inline} and finishes at [\\(a\\otimes(b\\otimes(c\\otimes
d))\\)]{.math .inline}: two factorizations of one map.

Why are there two hexagon equations rather than one?

Braiding must clear composites on either side. One equation moves a
single object past a composite; the other moves a composite past a
single object; together the two equations cover both sides.

Verify that
[\\(M\^{\\sigma\\sigma}\_{1}=\\theta_1/\\theta\_\\sigma\^2\\)]{.math
.inline} using the listed phases.

[\\(R\^{\\sigma\\sigma}\_{1}=e\^{-i\\pi/8}\\)]{.math .inline} squares to
[\\(e\^{-i\\pi/4}\\)]{.math .inline}, while
[\\(\\theta_1/\\theta\_\\sigma\^2=1/e\^{i\\pi/4}=e\^{-i\\pi/4}\\)]{.math
.inline}.

State the consequence of omitting the pentagon equation.

A four-anyon amplitude can then depend on the selected sequence of
intermediate basis changes. The symbols no longer define a single linear
map.
:::
::::

[← Appendix D --- Four charges and a table of
crossings](#appendix-d-four-charges-and-a-table-of-crossings)[Appendix F
--- Unitary elimination of high-energy subspaces
→](#appendix-f-unitary-elimination-of-high-energy-subspaces)

## Appendix F --- Unitary elimination of high-energy subspaces

Chapter 37 explained effective couplings as excursions into high-energy
states and back. This appendix turns that picture into an operator
calculation: a Schrieffer--Wolff rotation re-bases the full Hilbert
space so the low-energy block stands alone through a chosen perturbative
order, keeping exactly the return-trip corrections that bare projection
drops. The reference for conditions and error bounds is [Bravyi,
DiVincenzo, and Loss](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.0675).

Background, scope, and supporting argument

::: {.detail-body math-section=""}
An earlier calculation compressed two low-energy states plus one
high-energy state into an effective [\\(2\\times 2\\)]{.math .inline}
matrix, whose induced coupling came out as [\\(-g\^2/\\Delta\\)]{.math
.inline}: coupling squared over gap, with a minus sign from the energy
denominator.

No high-energy eigenstate survives in the reduced description. The
excitation survives only as an energy denominator suppressing the
induced coupling.

That three-state example generalizes to a whole low-energy family ---
including a degenerate family sharing one unperturbed energy. This
appendix derives the rotation in general and then evaluates it in closed
form for the two-site Hubbard model.

Deleting the high-energy basis vectors gives a different, cruder answer:
truncation keeps only processes staying inside the low sector and drops
every excursion that leaves it and returns.

The remedy is a unitary rotation --- a norm-preserving change of basis
--- applied to the full space before truncating the [\\(Q\\)]{.math
.inline} block. The rotation decouples the [\\(P\\)]{.math .inline} low
block from the [\\(Q\\)]{.math .inline} high block order by order;
truncating after the rotation keeps the excursion effects inside the
retained block.

    before rotation after rotation

    P states Q states P block | 0
    --------+-------
    0 | Q block

When several retained states share one unperturbed energy, single-state
perturbation theory encounters zero energy differences. Degenerate
perturbation theory therefore rotates the whole [\\(P\\)]{.math .inline}
family as one block while the [\\(Q\\)]{.math .inline} family remains
eliminated; the correction acts on an unperturbed eigenspace of
dimension greater than one rather than on an individual state.
:::

::: chapter-tools
Show detailed notes
:::

:::: {.section .topic aria-labelledby="f.1-decomposition-into-retained-and-eliminated-subspaces" math-section=""}
### F.1 Decomposition into Retained and Eliminated Subspaces

Write [\\(H=H_0+\\lambda V\\)]{.math .inline}, where [\\(H_0\\)]{.math
.inline} has a known isolated low-energy subspace and
[\\(\\lambda\\)]{.math .inline} is a bookkeeping parameter. Let
[\\(P\\)]{.math .inline} project onto the low subspace and
[\\(Q\\)]{.math .inline} onto everything orthogonal to it:

[\\\[ P\^2 = P, \\quad Q\^2 = Q, \\quad PQ = 0, \\quad P + Q = I
\\\]]{.math .display}

Detailed treatment: decomposition into retained and eliminated subspaces

::: {.detail-body math-section=""}
#### Decomposition into retained and eliminated subspaces

Cut the Hilbert space with two complementary operators [\\(P\\)]{.math
.inline} and [\\(Q\\)]{.math .inline}: orthogonal projectors selecting
mutually orthogonal subspaces, satisfying

[\\\[ P\^2=P,\\qquad Q\^2=Q,\\qquad PQ=0,\\qquad P+Q=I. \\\]]{.math
.display}

The identity [\\(I\\)]{.math .inline} is their sum. The range of
[\\(P\\)]{.math .inline} is the retained low sector; the range of
[\\(Q\\)]{.math .inline} is the eliminated high sector. The Hamiltonian
plus its perturbation reads

[\\\[ H=H_0+\\lambda V, \\\]]{.math .display}

where [\\(H_0\\)]{.math .inline} diagonalizes explicitly,
[\\(V\\)]{.math .inline} is Hermitian and carries units of energy, and
[\\(\\lambda\\)]{.math .inline} is the dimensionless power-counter for
the expansion. Once the series is truncated and the physical small ratio
identified, [\\(\\lambda\\)]{.math .inline} returns to one.

Start with the degenerate case: every retained state shares one
unperturbed energy [\\(E_0\\)]{.math .inline}:

[\\\[ PH_0P=E_0P, \\\]]{.math .display}

with no eigenvalue of [\\(QH_0Q\\)]{.math .inline} equal to
[\\(E_0\\)]{.math .inline}: the retained level stands clear of the
eliminated spectrum. Their separation is the gap

[\\\[ \\Delta_0=\\min\_{\\mu\\in Q}\|E\_\\mu-E_0\|\>0, \\\]]{.math
.display}

with [\\(E\_\\mu\\)]{.math .inline} running over the [\\(H_0\\)]{.math
.inline} eigenvalues inside [\\(Q\\)]{.math .inline}. A nonzero gap in
[\\(H_0\\)]{.math .inline} makes the resolvent
[\\((E_0-QH_0Q)\^{-1}\\)]{.math .inline} a well-defined operator on
[\\(Q\\)]{.math .inline}. A closing gap destroys that inverse, which
signals the cut between [\\(P\\)]{.math .inline} and [\\(Q\\)]{.math
.inline} was drawn in the wrong place.

Every operator splits into a block-diagonal piece staying inside
[\\(P\\)]{.math .inline} or inside [\\(Q\\)]{.math .inline}, plus an
off-diagonal piece crossing between them. For the perturbation that
split reads

[\\\[ V\_{\\rm d}=PVP+QVQ, \\qquad V\_{\\rm od}=PVQ+QVP. \\\]]{.math
.display}

The off-diagonal piece [\\(V\_{\\rm od}\\)]{.math .inline} is the bridge
between the sectors. Bare projection [\\(PHP\\)]{.math .inline} drops
that bridge, keeping only stay-at-home processes. The rotation below
folds the leave-and-return excursions back into the retained block.
:::
::::

:::: {.section .topic aria-labelledby="f.2-the-schrieffer-wolff-transformation" math-section=""}
### F.2 The Schrieffer-Wolff Transformation

Pick an anti-Hermitian generator [\\(S\\)]{.math .inline} ---
[\\(S\^\\dagger=-S\\)]{.math .inline}, so its exponential is unitary ---
to rotate [\\(e\^SHe\^{-S}\\)]{.math .inline} toward block-diagonal
form, order by order. The retained block then carries the excursion
corrections inside ordinary low-energy matrix elements.

The displayed formula covers the degenerate case
[\\(PH_0P=E_0P\\)]{.math .inline}, with retained energy
[\\(E_0\\)]{.math .inline}. Its resolvent acts only inside
[\\(Q\\)]{.math .inline}, where the gap keeps it finite. A retained band
of finite width requires the quasi-degenerate extension developed in the
detailed treatment below.

Through second order the retained block reads:

[\\\[ H\_{\\mathrm{eff}} = E_0P + \\lambda PVP + \\lambda\^2 PVQ
\\frac{1}{E_0 - QH_0Q} QVP + O(\\lambda\^3) \\\]]{.math .display}

Read the second-order term right to left as a three-step excursion:
[\\(QVP\\)]{.math .inline} hops from the retained sector into the
excluded sector; the resolvent weights the visit by its energy
denominator; [\\(PVQ\\)]{.math .inline} hops back. In an excluded
eigenbasis that excursion is

[\\\[ \\langle a\|H\_{\\mathrm{eff}}\^{(2)}\|b\\rangle
=\\lambda\^2\\sum\_{m\\in Q} \\frac{\\langle a\|V\|m\\rangle\\langle
m\|V\|b\\rangle}{E_0-E_m}. \\\]]{.math .display}

With all excluded levels above [\\(E_0\\)]{.math .inline} every
denominator is negative --- but the sign of a given effective coupling
still depends on the numerator matrix elements as well. Collapsing all
denominators to one gap and all numerators to one scale yields an
order-of-magnitude estimate, not the coupling.

Detailed treatment: perturbative block diagonalization

::: {.detail-body math-section=""}
#### Perturbative block diagonalization

Choose an anti-Hermitian generator [\\(S\\)]{.math .inline} with
[\\(S\^\\dagger=-S\\)]{.math .inline}, connecting only the two subspaces
--- no block-diagonal part:

[\\\[ PSP=QSQ=0. \\\]]{.math .display}

Exponentiation gives the unitary [\\(U=e\^S\\)]{.math .inline}. The
rotated Hamiltonian is

[\\\[ \\widetilde H=e\^SHe\^{-S}. \\\]]{.math .display}

Conjugation expands in nested commutators --- the
Baker--Campbell--Hausdorff series:

[\\\[ \\widetilde H=H+\[S,H\]+\\frac{1}{2!}\[S,\[S,H\]\]+\\cdots,
\\\]]{.math .display}

with [\\(\[A,B\]=AB-BA\\)]{.math .inline}. Expand the generator in
powers of the bookkeeping parameter:

[\\\[ S=\\lambda S_1+\\lambda\^2S_2+\\cdots. \\\]]{.math .display}

Collecting the terms linear in [\\(\\lambda\\)]{.math .inline}, the
surviving off-diagonal piece is

[\\\[ \\lambda\\bigl(V\_{\\rm od}+\[S_1,H_0\]\\bigr). \\\]]{.math
.display}

It vanishes by the choice

[\\\[ \[H_0,S_1\]=V\_{\\rm od}. \\\]]{.math .display}

For [\\(\|a\\rangle\\)]{.math .inline} in [\\(P\\)]{.math .inline} and
[\\(\|\\mu\\rangle\\)]{.math .inline} in [\\(Q\\)]{.math .inline}, the
condition reads in components

[\\\[ \\langle a\|S_1\|\\mu\\rangle =\\frac{\\langle
a\|V\|\\mu\\rangle}{E_0-E\_\\mu}. \\\]]{.math .display}

Anti-Hermiticity fixes the reverse element [\\(S_1\\)]{.math .inline}.
Projecting the rotated Hamiltonian back into [\\(P\\)]{.math .inline}
gives the retained block through second order:

[\\\[ \\boxed{ H\_{\\rm eff}=E_0P+\\lambda PVP
+\\lambda\^2PVQ\\frac{1}{E_0-QH_0Q}QVP +O(\\lambda\^3). } \\\]]{.math
.display}

Here [\\(O(\\lambda\^3)\\)]{.math .inline} collects all terms of third
and higher order in [\\(\\lambda\\)]{.math .inline}. The effective
Hamiltonian is thus no new physical system: it is one block of the
rotated full Hamiltonian, viewed in the rotated basis.

The boxed block is Hermitian, and its second-order term narrates the
excursion: out of [\\(P\\)]{.math .inline} via [\\(V\\)]{.math .inline},
dwell in [\\(Q\\)]{.math .inline} weighted by the resolvent, back via
[\\(V\\)]{.math .inline}. The units check out as

[\\\[ \[V\]\\,\[E\^{-1}\]\\,\[V\]=E\\,E\^{-1}E=E. \\\]]{.math .display}

With [\\(E\_\\mu\>E_0\\)]{.math .inline} each denominator
[\\(E_0-E\_\\mu\<0\\)]{.math .inline} is negative, so a coupled
low-energy state typically shifts downward at second order. The word
"virtual" alone does not fix that sign; the denominator does. Here
"virtual" means one thing: the intermediate visit occupies a state
outside the retained subspace. The many-body version with locality and
error bounds is developed by Bravyi, DiVincenzo, and Loss
[\[R025\]](#ref-R025 "[R025] Sergey Bravyi, David P. DiVincenzo, and Daniel Loss,
“Schrieffer–Wolff transformation for quantum many-body systems,” Annals
of Physics 326, 2793–2826 (2011)."){.citation}.

Decoupling [\\(P\\)]{.math .inline} from [\\(Q\\)]{.math .inline} order
by order, without touching the exact spectrum, is the Schrieffer--Wolff
transformation. The name comes from the original Anderson-to-Kondo
application; current usage covers any low-energy block coupled to
high-energy states
[\[R024\]](#ref-R024 "[R024] J. R. Schrieffer and P. A. Wolff, “Relation between the
Anderson and Kondo Hamiltonians,” Physical Review 149, 491–492 (1966).
DOI: 10.1103/PhysRev.149.491 ."){.citation};
[\[R025\]](#ref-R025 "[R025] Sergey Bravyi, David P. DiVincenzo, and Daniel Loss,
“Schrieffer–Wolff transformation for quantum many-body systems,” Annals
of Physics 326, 2793–2826 (2011)."){.citation}.

When the retained band has finite width, write [\\(\|a\\rangle\\)]{.math
.inline} and [\\(\|b\\rangle\\)]{.math .inline} in [\\(P\\)]{.math
.inline} with their own unperturbed energies [\\(E_a\\)]{.math .inline}
and [\\(E_b\\)]{.math .inline}. The Hermitian second-order form --- the
average of the two one-sided denominators --- is

[\\\[ (H\_{\\rm eff}\^{(2)})\_{ab} =\\frac12\\sum\_{\\mu\\in
Q}V\_{a\\mu}V\_{\\mu b} \\left( \\frac{1}{E_a-E\_\\mu}+
\\frac{1}{E_b-E\_\\mu} \\right). \\\]]{.math .display}

Here [\\(V\_{a\\mu}=\\langle a\|V\|\\mu\\rangle\\)]{.math .inline}.
Setting [\\(E_a=E_b=E_0\\)]{.math .inline} collapses both denominators
to the boxed form. Other conventions for the effective Hamiltonian
rotate the result by a unitary acting only inside [\\(P\\)]{.math
.inline}; spectra and consistently rotated observables then agree
through the retained order
[\[R025\]](#ref-R025 "[R025] Sergey Bravyi, David P. DiVincenzo, and Daniel Loss,
“Schrieffer–Wolff transformation for quantum many-body systems,” Annals
of Physics 326, 2793–2826 (2011)."){.citation}.
:::
::::

::::::::::: {.section .topic aria-labelledby="f.3-the-two-site-hubbard-model" math-section=""}
### F.3 The Two-Site Hubbard Model

Two sites share two electrons with repulsive on-site cost
[\\(U\>0\\)]{.math .inline} per double occupancy and hopping amplitude
[\\(t\\)]{.math .inline} between sites. At half filling with
[\\(\|t\|\\ll U\\)]{.math .inline} the low sector holds one electron per
site. One hop creates a doubly occupied site at cost [\\(U\\)]{.math
.inline}; the second hop returns to the singly occupied sector.

Only the singlet can make that round trip, as the Pauli analysis below
shows; the triplets are blocked. With dimensionless
spin-[\\(1/2\\)]{.math .inline} operators the second-order retained
block is:

[\\\[ H\_{\\mathrm{eff}}\^{(2)} = J \\left( \\mathbf S_1 \\cdot \\mathbf
S_2 - \\frac{1}{4} n_1 n_2 \\right), \\quad J = \\frac{4t\^2}{U} \> 0
\\\]]{.math .display}

Inside the singly occupied sector [\\(n_1n_2=1\\)]{.math .inline}, so
the operator reduces to numbers on the two spin sectors: the singlet
([\\(\\mathbf S_1\\cdot\\mathbf S_2=-3/4\\)]{.math .inline}) shifts by
[\\(-J\\)]{.math .inline}; each triplet ([\\(+1/4\\)]{.math .inline})
shifts by zero. The positive exchange coefficient thus lowers the
singlet below the triplets. That spin splitting from round-trip charge
motion is superexchange.

Defect-cluster gadgets borrow this round-trip logic, but each gadget
needs its own matrix elements and a full accounting of competing terms:
the two-site value fixes no four-body coefficient.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Detailed treatment: two-site Hubbard superexchange

::: {.detail-body math-section=""}
#### Two-site Hubbard superexchange

Consider two sites, labeled [\\(1\\)]{.math .inline} and [\\(2\\)]{.math
.inline}, with one spin-[\\(1/2\\)]{.math .inline} fermion per site. A
fermion is a particle whose creation and annihilation operators obey
anticommutation relations. Let [\\(c\_{i\\sigma}\^\\dagger\\)]{.math
.inline} create a fermion of spin
[\\(\\sigma\\in\\{\\uparrow,\\downarrow\\}\\)]{.math .inline} at site
[\\(i\\)]{.math .inline}, and define the corresponding occupation-number
operator by [\\(n\_{i\\sigma}=c\_{i\\sigma}\^\\dagger
c\_{i\\sigma}\\)]{.math .inline}. The two-site Hubbard Hamiltonian is
divided into

[\\\[ H_0=U\\sum\_{i=1}\^2n\_{i\\uparrow}n\_{i\\downarrow}, \\\]]{.math
.display}

[\\\[ V=-t\\sum\_{\\sigma} \\left(c\_{1\\sigma}\^\\dagger c\_{2\\sigma}
+c\_{2\\sigma}\^\\dagger c\_{1\\sigma}\\right). \\\]]{.math .display}

The on-site repulsion [\\(U\>0\\)]{.math .inline} is the energy cost of
placing two fermions on the same site, and the hopping amplitude
[\\(t\\)]{.math .inline} controls motion between the sites. Both
[\\(U\\)]{.math .inline} and [\\(t\\)]{.math .inline} have units of
energy. The retained subspace [\\(P\\)]{.math .inline} contains states
with exactly one fermion on each site, so [\\(E_0=0\\)]{.math .inline}.

The eliminated subspace [\\(Q\\)]{.math .inline} contains states with
one doubly occupied site and one empty site. These states have energy
[\\(U\\)]{.math .inline}. The perturbative assumption is

[\\\[ \|t\|/U\\ll1. \\\]]{.math .display}

The first-order contribution vanishes because one hop always takes a
state out of the one-particle-per-site sector. Thus [\\(PVP=0\\)]{.math
.inline}. At second order,

[\\\[ H\_{\\rm eff}\^{(2)}=-\\frac{1}{U}PVQVP. \\\]]{.math .display}

Introduce the spin operator on site [\\(i\\)]{.math .inline},

[\\\[ \\mathbf S_i=\\frac12\\sum\_{\\alpha,\\beta}
c\_{i\\alpha}\^\\dagger\\boldsymbol\\sigma\_{\\alpha\\beta}c\_{i\\beta},
\\\]]{.math .display}

where [\\(\\boldsymbol\\sigma=(X,Y,Z)\\)]{.math .inline} collects the
three Pauli matrices. Summing the two-hop paths over intermediate sites
and spins gives
[\[R026\]](#ref-R026 "[R026] A. H. MacDonald, S. M. Girvin, and D. Yoshioka, “ \(t/U\) expansion for the Hubbard model,”
Physical Review B 37, 9753–9756 (1988)."){.citation}

[\\\[ H\_{\\rm eff}\^{(2)}= \\frac{4t\^2}{U} \\left(\\mathbf
S_1\\cdot\\mathbf S_2-\\frac14n_1n_2\\right), \\\]]{.math .display}

where [\\(n_i=n\_{i\\uparrow}+n\_{i\\downarrow}\\)]{.math .inline}.
Within [\\(P\\)]{.math .inline}, each site is singly occupied, so
[\\(n_1n_2=1\\)]{.math .inline}.

Define the exchange coefficient

[\\\[ J\_{\\rm ex}=4t\^2/U. \\\]]{.math .display}

For the spin singlet, [\\(\\mathbf S_1\\cdot\\mathbf S_2=-3/4\\)]{.math
.inline}, and the second-order energy shift is [\\(-J\_{\\rm
ex}=-4t\^2/U\\)]{.math .inline}.

For any triplet, [\\(\\mathbf S_1\\cdot\\mathbf S_2=+1/4\\)]{.math
.inline}, and the corresponding shift is zero. The singlet--triplet
separation is therefore

[\\\[ \\Delta\_{ST}=\\frac{4t\^2}{U}. \\\]]{.math .display}

The result is antiferromagnetic superexchange: virtual hops through
doubly occupied states leave behind a spin coupling favoring the
singlet. The coupling is no new microscopic hopping: it is two hops
times one denominator [\\(U\\)]{.math .inline}. Written as
[\\(4t(t/U)\\)]{.math .inline} it is visibly smaller than bare hopping
by the small ratio [\\(\|t\|/U\\ll1\\)]{.math .inline}.

Pauli exclusion separates the two cases. A triplet carries symmetric
spin, so its spatial part is antisymmetric --- and that antisymmetry
blocks the on-site double occupancy the round trip needs.

The singlet carries the complementary spatial symmetry, so its round
trip proceeds and its energy drops. The symmetry argument and the
explicit two-hop algebra agree.
:::

::: {.section .topic-extension math-section=""}
#### Procedure for validating an effective Hamiltonian

On a finite-dimensional problem, build and check the effective
Hamiltonian through the following steps. Each step has a failure mode
worth naming.

- Choose the projector [\\(P\\)]{.math .inline} by energy scales:
  include every state whose splittings are comparable to the
  perturbation. Leaving a near-resonant state outside shrinks a
  denominator instead of simplifying the theory.

- Diagonalize [\\(PVP\\)]{.math .inline} first: within an exactly
  degenerate manifold its eigenvectors are the correct zeroth-order
  combinations.

- Construct the resolvent [\\((E_0-QH_0Q)\^{-1}\\)]{.math .inline} ---
  the inverse operator packaging all intermediate-state energy
  denominators --- acting only on [\\(Q\\)]{.math .inline}. Each
  eliminated-state contribution enters divided by its excitation-energy
  difference.

- Assemble [\\(H\_{\\rm eff}\\)]{.math .inline} order by order, keeping
  every operator the order produces --- including unwelcome fields and
  bare constants.

- Rotate observables with the same unitary. For a microscopic observable
  [\\(O\\)]{.math .inline} the consistent effective operator is [\\\[
  O\_{\\rm eff}=Pe\^SOe\^{-S}P. \\\]]{.math .display} while bare
  truncation [\\(POP\\)]{.math .inline} drops the virtual-transition
  corrections.

- Benchmark the effective model against the full Hamiltonian on the
  smallest tractable cluster: low-energy eigenvalues, spectral subspaces
  (not just individual eigenvectors), and rotated observables, tracked
  as [\\(\|\\lambda\|\\)]{.math .inline} varies.

The expansion is controlled when the coupling matrix elements between
[\\(P\\)]{.math .inline} and [\\(Q\\)]{.math .inline} are small against
the relevant denominators. On a finite cluster that condition is
summarized by the dimensionless ratio [\\(\\\|V\_{\\rm
od}\\\|/\\Delta_0\\)]{.math .inline}, with [\\(\\\|\\cdot\\\|\\)]{.math
.inline} the operator norm.

On an extended lattice the full perturbation norm grows with volume, so
the global ratio overestimates the danger. Rigorous bounds use locality
and linked-cluster structure instead of the extensive norm alone
[\[R025\]](#ref-R025 "[R025] Sergey Bravyi, David P. DiVincenzo, and Daniel Loss,
“Schrieffer–Wolff transformation for quantum many-body systems,” Annals
of Physics 326, 2793–2826 (2011)."){.citation}. A large global norm
still allows a controlled local expansion, while one small bond does not
certify control.

Existence and accuracy are separate questions. The existence question
asks whether some exact unitary maps the perturbed low-energy spectral
subspace back onto the reference [\\(P\\)]{.math .inline}.

For a finite-dimensional problem whose isolated band stays isolated
under the perturbation, that unitary exists, which is the geometric fact
behind exact Schrieffer--Wolff theory
[\[R025\]](#ref-R025 "[R025] Sergey Bravyi, David P. DiVincenzo, and Daniel Loss,
“Schrieffer–Wolff transformation for quantum many-body systems,” Annals
of Physics 326, 2793–2826 (2011)."){.citation};
[\[R027\]](#ref-R027 "[R027] T. Kato, Perturbation Theory for Linear Operators, 2nd ed.,
Springer (1976; corrected printing 1995). DOI: 10.1007/978-3-642-66282-9 ."){.citation}.
The accuracy question is whether a short Taylor series captures that
unitary well enough at the retained order.

Accuracy needs its own evidence: a small parameter plus a direct
truncation check. An exact rotation can exist while the second-order
formula still fails.

An effective Hamiltonian carries two redundancies: an overall additive
constant and a unitary basis choice inside [\\(P\\)]{.math .inline}.
Constants shift all levels together, leaving dynamics and gaps
untouched.

Basis rotations inside [\\(P\\)]{.math .inline} shuffle individual
matrix entries, so two derivations can print different-looking
Hamiltonians for the same physics. Compare in the invariant-first order:
spectra first, then observables rotated under the same convention, and
only then individual terms.

A many-body effective Hamiltonian can print a term shaped like a
toric-code check operator. That resemblance is one term among many:
topological order is a property of the full low-energy spectrum ---
degeneracy, gaps, and excitations --- and needs that whole-spectrum
analysis.

Gadget constructions that cancel the first several orders deliberately
live on a knife-edge: record the surviving coefficient together with the
leading omitted term and every symmetry-breaking term the cancellation
leaves behind. Before trusting the gadget at scale, check its spectrum
against the full Hamiltonian on the smallest exactly diagonalizable
cluster.

A controlled order-[\\(m\\)]{.math .inline} approximation improves by
one power of the small parameter per added order, over an interval where
the parameter is genuinely small. Two data points cannot fit that
exponent reliably.

Compare retained subspaces with projectors, not single vectors:
individual eigenvectors inside a degenerate manifold rotate freely while
the subspace stands still.

The original Schrieffer--Wolff calculation related the Anderson and
Kondo descriptions
[\[R024\]](#ref-R024 "[R024] J. R. Schrieffer and P. A. Wolff, “Relation between the
Anderson and Kondo Hamiltonians,” Physical Review 149, 491–492 (1966).
DOI: 10.1103/PhysRev.149.491 ."){.citation}. Modern rigorous treatments
use the same warning in the other direction: the method never licenses
keeping only terms judged desirable
[\[R025\]](#ref-R025 "[R025] Sergey Bravyi, David P. DiVincenzo, and Daniel Loss,
“Schrieffer–Wolff transformation for quantum many-body systems,” Annals
of Physics 326, 2793–2826 (2011)."){.citation}.
:::

Common errors in Schrieffer--Wolff reductions

:::: {.detail-body math-section=""}
::: {.section .topic-extension math-section=""}
#### Common errors in Schrieffer--Wolff reductions

- Replacing the full Hamiltonian by bare truncation [\\(PHP\\)]{.math
  .inline} keeps only stay-at-home processes: it drops every excursion
  through [\\(Q\\)]{.math .inline} and with it the energy shifts and
  induced couplings those excursions generate.

- Drawing the cut so a near-resonant state falls outside [\\(P\\)]{.math
  .inline} breaks the assumed scale separation: under the perturbation
  that state can join the low-energy band, and its denominator collapses
  toward zero.

- A small typical bond establishes only local information, while an
  extensive global norm can coexist with a controlled local expansion;
  lattice-wide control requires local bounds.

- An exact block-diagonalizing unitary guarantees existence, not
  accuracy: the second-order formula still needs its own truncation
  check.

- Two effective Hamiltonians compared term by term under different bases
  inside [\\(P\\)]{.math .inline} can disagree on paper while describing
  the same physics; align the conventions first.

- Pairing the rotated Hamiltonian with unrotated microscopic observables
  drops the virtual corrections the same rotation would have added to
  them.

- A coveted fourth-order term can drown in an unnoticed first- or
  second-order field. Track every term at the order that generates it.

- Calling the rotated model an encoded code, a topological phase, or an
  anyon theory claims many-body properties the rotation alone cannot
  supply. Those properties belong to the resulting Hamiltonian and its
  states. The rotation builds candidate local degrees of freedom and
  interactions; the many-body analysis comes after.

Watch for drift on both sides of the fraction: a [\\(Q\\)]{.math
.inline} state can approach the retained energies from below, and
fabrication shifts can resize the numerator matrix elements and the
denominator gaps together.
:::
::::

Verification statements

:::: {.detail-body math-section=""}
::: {.section .topic-extension math-section=""}
#### Verification statements

- Keep the [\\(Q\\)]{.math .inline} states through the rotation:
  excursions through [\\(Q\\)]{.math .inline} shift energies and
  generate interactions inside [\\(P\\)]{.math .inline}.

- With [\\(E\_\\mu\>E_0\\)]{.math .inline} each resolvent entry
  [\\(1/(E_0-E\_\\mu)\<0\\)]{.math .inline} is negative, so the sandwich
  [\\(PVQ(\\cdots)QVP\\)]{.math .inline} corrects [\\(P\\)]{.math
  .inline} downward as a negative-semidefinite operator.

- Setting [\\(E_a=E_b=E_0\\)]{.math .inline} makes the two denominators
  equal, so their average is [\\(1/(E_0-E\_\\mu)\\)]{.math .inline} and
  the sum over [\\(\\mu\\)]{.math .inline} reassembles the matrix
  element of [\\(PVQ(E_0-QH_0Q)\^{-1}QVP\\)]{.math .inline}.

- The two-site scale [\\(4t\^2/U\\)]{.math .inline} assembles from four
  factors: two hops return the system to the retained sector, amplitudes
  multiply to [\\(t\^2\\)]{.math .inline}, the virtual double occupancy
  contributes the denominator [\\(U\\)]{.math .inline}, and
  spin-plus-path counting supplies the factor of four.

- The same unitary must be applied to observables and states alongside
  the Hamiltonian.

- A near-resonant state left outside [\\(P\\)]{.math .inline} brings a
  collapsing denominator: under the perturbation it can join the
  low-energy band.
:::
::::

[← Appendix E --- Consistency of alternative fusion

--- Stabilizer checks without logical-state measurement
→](#appendix-g-stabilizer-checks-without-logical-state-measurement)

## Appendix G --- Stabilizer checks without logical-state measurement

A stabilizer encoding stores information in the joint eigenspace of a
set of commuting checks. Measuring those checks reports which
constraints an error has violated, while leaving the encoded amplitudes
unresolved. Syndrome measurement therefore probes error relations; a
logical-state measurement probes an observable acting within the encoded
subspace.

Background, scope, and supporting argument

::: {.detail-body math-section=""}
Compare coin 1 with coin 2 and coin 2 with coin 3, recording whether
each pair agrees. If both comparisons report agreement, all three faces
match, but neither result tells whether the common face is heads or
tails. The undetermined common face is the information that the checks
preserve.

A general pure state of [\\(n\\)]{.math .inline} qubits needs
[\\(2\^n\\)]{.math .inline} complex amplitudes. Some important quantum
states admit a shorter description as a list of constraints. The
condition "all three bits agree," for example, selects the allowed
computational-basis strings directly instead of listing all eight
strings and assigning zero amplitude to six of them.
:::

Show detailed notes
